subsubtopic: DOOR-TO-DOOR MAIL DELIVERY IN URBAN AREAS-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise, under the provisions of Standing Order 43, on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity.
The city of Calgary is growing at the rate of more than
2,000	people per month. There are eight or more new, large districts in Calgary North and other areas where the Post Office has established postal depots, without boxes in many cases, and the depots are open only from eight o'clock in the morning to four o'clock in the afternoon. These new areas are made up mainly of young people from all parts of the country, and in many cases both spouses work and are unable to get their mail as the depots are locked by 4 p.m.. Family allowance cheques and personal mail are unobtainable.
Therefore, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Calgary Centre (Mr. Andre):	-
That the Postmaster General personally look into this serious situation and see that 4,000 boxes, unused and presently in the possession of the Post Office, are placed in these depots, and that the said depots remain open so that people, with or without keys, can obtain their mail after working hours; and, further, every effort should be made to see that all people get delivery of mail the same as established in other parts of the city of Calgary, in view of the present discriminatory policy, so that all taxpayers and Canadians have equal opportunity.

subsubtopic: CANADA SAVINGS BONDS-REQUESTED INCREASE IN INTEREST RATE-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity under the provisions of Standing Order 43.
In the past three weeks the redemption of Canada Savings Bonds has accelerated, and again last week Bank of Canada figures showed a net decline of $90 million for that week, according to The Globe and Mail. This compares with $52 million the previous week and $22 million the week before. The average last year at this time was running at just $10 million. I move, seconded by the hon. member for Brant (Mr. Blackburn):
That in view of the fact many of the owners of these bonds are just plain, ordinary Canadian citizens, the Canadian government increase the interest rates on these bonds to protect these ordinary citizens and/or consider seriously indexing these bond issues to the consumer price index.

subsubtopic: APPOINTMENT OF NEW DEPUTY MINISTER-EFFECT ON POLICY OF DEPARTMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Prime Minister and touches upon his announcement yesterday of the appointment of a new deputy minister to the Department of Finance.
In view of the fact that in the past decade our budget surplus of $393 million has gone to a budget deficit of $12.1 billion, that the current account surplus nine years ago of $1.1 billion is now $4.4 billion, that unemployment is up 50 per cent and inflation is now at 9 per cent, compared to 3.3 per cent, with bankruptcies up dramatically, will the Prime Minister indicate if the appointment of the new deputy minister yesterday was in anticipation of a change in direction as far as the Department of Finance is concerned?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):

With regard to that general subject, would the Prime Minister indicate if the promotion of Mr. Shoyama to the position of special adviser in his own office is a further indication of the downgrading of the Department of Finance and the upgrading of the Prime Minister's office to deal with questions of the economy?

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister is always complaining that he is being taken out of context, yet he repeatedly takes the Leader of the Opposition out of context when he refers to questions of the deficit.

subtopic: STEPS TO REDUCE NUMBER OF BANKRUPTCIES
STEPS TO REDUCE NUMBER OF BANKRUPTCIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a supplementary question for the Prime Minister, but perhaps I should repeat the question asked by my colleague.
In view of the fact that the Prime Minister, three months ago, said that he would be taking some specific steps in looking at the bankruptcy rates within our economy, what steps, in fact, has he taken during this period of time?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subtopic: STEPS TO REDUCE NUMBER OF BANKRUPTCIES
speechtext: None, Mr. Speaker.

subtopic: STEPS TO REDUCE NUMBER OF BANKRUPTCIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is very obvious that the government has taken no steps to deal with the bankruptcy rates in Canada. But if the Prime Minister is not doing anything about the situation, I would like to put a question to the Minister of Finance.
In view of the fact that the business rate in Canada increased by 41.1 per cent in 1978 over 1977, would the minister be prepared, particularly within the small business sector, to look into areas which would reduce the bankruptcy rate-for example, amendments to the Small Businesses Loans Act?

subtopic: STEPS TO REDUCE NUMBER OF BANKRUPTCIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we put certain measures in our last budget in order to help small businesses in Canada. For example, we changed the rules regarding capital gains and small businesses are now taxed at a rate which is half that of big business rates. It is a much better rate than their counterparts have in the United States. The legislation for small businesses in Canada is very good, and I am supported in that by Mr. John Bulloch who was very happy with what was done for small businesses in the last bill.

January 26, 1979
Oral Questions
Of course, when operating in an open economy as opposed to a controlled economy everyone takes their chance, and if the competition is very strong-a situation which everybody prefers-then some businesses will fail. It is what we call a market economy.

subtopic: STEPS TO REDUCE NUMBER OF BANKRUPTCIES
speechtext:
A supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. Is it not a fact that the Small Businesses Loans Act is not operating as effectively as was expected? In fact, a recent poll indicated that 95 per cent of small businesses applying for assistance were turned down.
Could the minister advise whether he has taken this matter up with the banks and, if not, would he now be prepared to do so in order that the small business sector may have an opportunity to take advantage of the act?

subtopic: STEPS TO REDUCE NUMBER OF BANKRUPTCIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will certainly be willing to look into the matter and talk to the banks, but I think there is a lot of credit available in Canada. In fact, for the third year savings in Canada are at a very high point.
I am told that the liquidity of the banks and other financial institutions is very good. In fact, not long ago one of the banks increased the rate for mortgages and then decided to put it back because there was too much competition. I think, therefore, that there is a lot of money available in the banking system for big business and also for small business. If there is some special problem that the hon. member wants to refer to, however, he can indicate it to me and I will talk to the banks.

subsubtopic: FUNDING OF OUTREACH PROGRAM-REQUEST PROGRAM BE CONTINUED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Minister of Employment and Immigration which concerns the Outreach program and particularly women.
On January 18, the Saskatoon, Saskatchewan, Outreach program that was specifically directed at women received a notice that the funding would be terminated as of March 31. As the minister knows, that program aided hundreds of singleparent families and many hundreds of women in the last year in Saskatoon: it helped get people off welfare and found them work.
Will the minister reverse the decision of his department, make sure the program is not cancelled and that funding will continue for the Saskatoon Outreach program which is so valuable?

speakeroldname: Hon. Bud Cullen (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
subsubtopic: FUNDING OF OUTREACH PROGRAM-REQUEST PROGRAM BE CONTINUED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the department recognized it was providing a valuable service. In fact, over the last years we have provided $191,000-close to $200,000 in funding.

We have done a survey of the various projects, however, and it was the feeling of regional officers that this particular service could be adequately performed on a cost-benefit basis by the Canada-Employment centre in that region and that a comparable service could be offered to women in the region.

subsubtopic: FUNDING OF OUTREACH PROGRAM-REQUEST PROGRAM BE CONTINUED
speechtext: A supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. There are some 21 other programs that are similar in national scope across the country. Since the minister will not save the program in Saskatoon, can he assure the House that the other 21 programs will not be cut back and, indeed, will not be terminated but will continue to provide the excellent service they have given in those communities?

subsubtopic: FUNDING OF OUTREACH PROGRAM-REQUEST PROGRAM BE CONTINUED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, these have all been looked at and some are in the process of being looked at. In some areas they will be continued with exactly the same funding, in other areas the project will be continued with less funding, while some will be cancelled as is the case with the one raised by the hon. member.
We are giving a close and careful look to each Outreach project with a view to determining which should be funded at the full level, at a reduced level, or cancelled altogether.

subsubtopic: FUNDING OF OUTREACH PROGRAM-REQUEST PROGRAM BE CONTINUED
speechtext: A final supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. The minister may add that the Outreach program in his own riding, as I understand it, is getting increased funding. I should like to ask the minister why, when he makes these decisions, he does not consult the head of the women's employment division in his department or the people involved in the training and development program. The information I have is that these people have not been consulted, and they have the direct knowledge of the value of these programs to women. Why have they not been consulted?

subsubtopic: FUNDING OF OUTREACH PROGRAM-REQUEST PROGRAM BE CONTINUED
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I shall have to check the allegation of the hon. member. I know that we have had a co-ordinator in this particular area since 1972, and it would be strange if that individual was not consulted. I will check to find out if that is the case.

subtopic: REPORT OF ADVISORY COUNCIL ON THE STATUS OF WOMEN- EMPLOYMENT STRATEGY
REPORT OF ADVISORY COUNCIL ON THE STATUS OF WOMEN- EMPLOYMENT STRATEGY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a supplementary question for the Minister of Employment and Immigration. Has the Minister had an opportunity to study the remarks made earlier this week, and the report of the chairman of the Advisory Council on the Status of Women published on January 10, with respect to the failure to involve the Advisory Council in the evolution of the employment strategy of the minister's department?
Has he conferred directly with the chairman or other representatives of the Advisory Council because of the very serious allegations raised about the lack of consultation and lack of input in terms of the formulation of employment policies and their impact upon women?
January 26, 1979

speakeroldname: Hon. Bud Cullen (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
subtopic: REPORT OF ADVISORY COUNCIL ON THE STATUS OF WOMEN- EMPLOYMENT STRATEGY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in answer to the first part of the hon. member's question, I have not had an opportunity to meet with the chairman, Mrs. Rousseau, but in fact at the committee, when they were talking about job creation and encouraging workers to establish more stable work patterns, she indicated:
The government may achieve this goal, not by reducing the benefits of the workers who are more likely to be affected by the a high unemployment rate, but rather by guaranteeing reasonable jobs and adequate training programs for women. The CACSW will go on studying very closely the employment strategy suggested by the government to inform women of their rights and job opportunities.
So, in fact, they have been studying the employment strategies: they have been looking at them and they have indicated that they are going to continue to do so. If there are representations to be made, they can be made. Mrs. Rousseau said:
Women are full-fledged members of the labour force with the right to the same opportunities and advantages as their male colleagues on the work force.
And, Mr. Speaker, Mrs. Rousseau was quoting me.

subtopic: REPORT OF ADVISORY COUNCIL ON THE STATUS OF WOMEN- EMPLOYMENT STRATEGY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I wonder if the minister would give this House an undertaking because of the very serious concerns raised about the lack of present consultation. Would he consult with his senior officials to see if there was any consultation with women or with the Advisory Council on the evolution of the employment strategy? Would he arrange, at the earliest possible date, a meeting in order to deal directly with the number of specific concerns that were raised at the recent quarterly meeting of the Advisory Council concerning the employment strategy and its impact upon women?

subtopic: REPORT OF ADVISORY COUNCIL ON THE STATUS OF WOMEN- EMPLOYMENT STRATEGY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as hon. members on both sides of the House know, my office door is open. I have met with many, many groups. There is never any difficulty getting in to see the Minister of Employment and Immigration, and I have received valuable assistance and advice from a whole series of groups in this particular field.
I will check with my officials to find out if there was some consultation or not on this specific matter. I am prepared, obviously, to meet with the president at any time she wishes in studying all the projects she says their group is going to undertake, and hear representations from them because they do have valuable points and ideas to put forward.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prince Albert):
subsubtopic: PROPOSED MOVE FROM HEATHROW TO GATWICK- REPRESENTATIONS TO U.K.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to direct a question to the Secretary of State for External Affairs. I am informed that he has made representations to the British government in connection with consideration being given by the government and the Board of Trade of the United Kingdom to switching air operations from the present Heathrow Airport to Gatwick. Air Canada, in consequence, will lose, in a little over 2Vi years, $270 million.
What representations have been made? What is the present position? Has the British government given an indication that it is prepared to reconsider its desire to shift the operations at these airports?

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald C. Jamieson (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: PROPOSED MOVE FROM HEATHROW TO GATWICK- REPRESENTATIONS TO U.K.
speechtext:
As briefly as I can, Mr. Speaker, the sequence is that this matter emerged some months ago between the Board of Trade, the appropriate government agency in Britain, and Air Canada. At that time Air Canada indicated its opposition to the move. That opposition was reinforced in representations which I and the Minister of Transport made to the then minister of the Board of Trade, Mr. Dell. Within the last few weeks the matter has been moved to a government-to-govern-ment basis as a result of conversations between our Prime Minister, Mr. Callaghan and others in December.

January 26, 1979
Oral Questions
The note which was referred to in the House a few days ago was delivered in person by our High Commissioner a week ago yesterday, I believe. Consequently, we are now awaiting the reaction of the British government. As of this morning, just shortly before coming into the House, no formal response- which, obviously, a formal note requires-had come from the British government. I stated in the House the other day, and I welcome this opportunity to reiterate it, that the Government of Canada agrees with Air Canada and will vigorously support all of its efforts to remain at Heathrow.

subsubtopic: PROPOSED MOVE FROM HEATHROW TO GATWICK- REPRESENTATIONS TO U.K.
speechtext: Would it not help in the deliberations that are taking place if this House were to pass a resolution strongly objecting to a course of action that will be so detrimental to Air Canada? Surely the House in general would be prepared to do that. If so, it would add strength to the representations being made by the High Commissioner.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: PROPOSED MOVE FROM HEATHROW TO GATWICK- REPRESENTATIONS TO U.K.
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, no one in the House is more aware of the sensitivities and sensibilities of the British government and British parliament on these matters. I will consider it, if it appears it would be advantageous to do so. Certainly, we on this side would have no objection. The only qualifying consideration would be whether or not the judgment on whether it would be beneficial is sustained. I will look at it over the weekend.

subtopic: MEASURES TO STIMULATE MANUFACTURING INDUSTRY AND REDUCE TRADE DEFICIT
MEASURES TO STIMULATE MANUFACTURING INDUSTRY AND REDUCE TRADE DEFICIT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce.
As the increase in our trade surplus last year was due solely to increased sales of our raw products, which provide relatively few jobs in their production and require absolutely no sales effort because of the great desire of other countries, particularly the United States, to obtain our raw products, and in view of the statement by Statistics Canada this morning that our trade deficit in fully manufactured products increased by 10 per cent during the past year to $12.2 billion from $11 billion in 1977, I ask the minister, will he not now come forward within the next week and announce to the House just what he is going to do to stimulate our manufacturing industry so that we can start to overcome this enormous trade deficit in fully manufactured products, the ones that produce the jobs?
I ask this especially in view of the fact that the Canadian Manufacturers' Association has stated that if we can overcome this enormous trade deficit, we can provide no less than
800,000	additional jobs for Canadians to work at, and completely eliminate unemployment in this country.

speakeroldname: Hon. Jack H. Horner (Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
subtopic: MEASURES TO STIMULATE MANUFACTURING INDUSTRY AND REDUCE TRADE DEFICIT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I just happen to have the music to answer the hon. member's question. Basically, manufacturing

jobs are up substantially in Canada this year over a year ago. Capacity utilization is up substantially, nearly 5 percentage points, over a year ago.
With regard to manufactured goods, I have the Statistics Canada figures with me. Imports of manufactured goods, inedible, are up 5.2 per cent. Our exports are up 24.5 per cent.

subtopic: MEASURES TO STIMULATE MANUFACTURING INDUSTRY AND REDUCE TRADE DEFICIT
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
subtopic: MEASURES TO STIMULATE MANUFACTURING INDUSTRY AND REDUCE TRADE DEFICIT
speechtext: I wish the hon. member would take a pencil and write these down. I have the exact figures for our imports of manufactured goods. The figure is $33,121 million for 1977. In 1978, imports of manufactured goods totalled $34,857 million. Compare that with the exports of our manufactured goods and the substantial increase is obvious. In 1977, we exported $30,042 million, and in 1978 we exported $37,412 million. That is a substantial increase in exports of manufactured goods. Naturally, this has been reflected in greater factory utilization and greater employment in the manufacturing field.

subsubtopic: MR. DIEFENBAKER-DELAY IN ANSWERING STARRED QUESTIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege. I have believed always that the essence of parliament is that questions, when they are asked, are answered within a reasonable time. I do not ask questions just for amusement. They have a basis in fact; otherwise they would not have been asked.
I intend to refer to three starred questions. On November 22 I placed question No. 610 on the order paper. It reads as follows:
1.	Has the Department of External Affairs set up an exercise known as "Program for Foreign Visitors"?
2.	Are funds available for foreigners touring Canada as "opinion formers"?
3.	How many of such "opinion formers" have toured Canada under the auspices of the Department of External Affairs, and what was the total cost in each of the past four years?
These are simple questions. These people were going across the country singing the Hallelujah chorus for the government.
Next, on November 22 I placed question No. 611 on the order paper. It reads as follows:
Privilege-Mr. Diefenbaker
1.	In consequence of Mr. Igor Gouzenko's revelations, how many individuals were prosecuted and (a) who were they (b) what happened in their respective cases?
2.	How many named in the revelations were not prosecuted and for what reason?
3.	With the termination of the 30 years during which secret documents are not revealed, for what reason is an exception being made in connection with his revelations?
Parliament has a right to that information, even though it might be uncomfortable for the government.
Also, on November 14 I placed question No. 576 on the order paper. It reads as follows:
1.	Was an order made that files containing secret or security information were not to be released until the expiry of 30 years and, if so, on what date?
2.	Has the government decided that all files in connection with the Gouzenko revelations of 1945-46 shall not be released now and, if so, for what reason and on what basis?
3.	Is the government aware of a press report that the reason given for non-production is "That they might hurt some people now living"?
4.	Were any such individuals then or thereafter or since cabinet ministers?
This series of questions does not require very much research. In every case this House has been denied the information; it has been delayed six or seven weeks. Why? If the government has nothing to hide, why hide it? What has happened here is a flagrant disregard and denial of parliament. There can be no excuse, excepting that the government does not want to reveal this information before the general election expected by me to be in April. Incidentally, I predicted that time for the election last October.
I want to have these questions answered. It may be understandable that there is diffidence on the part of the government to reveal the answers, but there is nothing in those questions which is not in the government's files and known to the government. I rise at this time simply to say that if we cannot receive information on matters which may be uncomfortable or even understandably viewed with suspicions by the government, then we might as well close down parliament. There have been some six, seven and eight weeks with no answers. I bring this to the attention of the House and I shall continue to do so regularly because I want this information before the election and not after.

This bill goes far beyond the particular problems we are facing today vis-a-vis the province of Quebec. It introduces a new device for constitutional change in respect of our provinces. I have some misgivings about this legislation which I should like to outline as quickly as possible within the limited time at my disposal. I hope the intervention by the hon. member opposite is not taken from my time.
Let me express certain misgivings I have because of this clearly very wide-ranging piece of legislation. As a result of statements by the responsible minister, and I say that in the legal sense as opposed to the actual sense, I have very serious misgivings as to how far this government intends to go with this legislation. Some of the clauses of this bill, specifically clause 3(1), provide in fact that referenda may be used for the discussion of constitutional matters. It is not a question of separation by any province, but a question of any constitutional matter. Clause 3 provides:
(1) Where it appears to the governor in council that any question relating to the Constitution of Canada or relating to or arising out of a proposed or possible change in the Constitution of Canada is of sufficient importance to warrant obtaining the opinion of electors on that question, the governor in council may, by proclamation, direct that the opinion of electors be obtained on that question by putting the question to the electors of Canada or of one or more provinces specified in the proclamation at a referendum called for that purpose.
Therefore, the government will define any question relating to the constitution, whether proposed or possible changes and whether in fact the matter is of sufficient importance. That is the reality of our parliamentary system. This power as to what issue is constitutional and of sufficient importance is left solely in the hands of the government of the day.
This government says that they are simply setting up the mechanics of a referendum and that parliament will be consulted. They then make provision for consultation, but is it a matter of introducing a bill where every aspect can be debated, or of using the normal parliamentary device and procedure of referring it to a committee before which parties or parliamentarians who are affected may come and argue their case, whether it be pro or con? What we have in this bill is the provision that we will magnanimously receive the opportunity to debate a resolution for 40 hours.
The leader of the New Democratic Party was ecstatic. He thinks that this is an amazing opportunity for us to examine the question with respect to the particular referendum. I suggest that that particular provision in itself is enough for people seriously to question this bill. Parliament in effect is being excluded from any specific question that has come foward with respect to a referendum in Canada. We know that the full extent of debate will be utilized by members supporting the government which put forward this legislation. There will be little opportunity for any minority points of view or for any dissent to be brought forward in the context of that kind of procedure.
I suggest that under the guise of bringing forward legislation, ostensibly to deal with the province of Quebec, the government is attempting to arm itself with powers regarding

As a parliamentarian I resent that, because I was elected by my constituents from a particular area of Canada to talk in terms of their aspirations and hopes within Canada. I do not want the interests of my constituents to be diminished or sidetracked, even if the government offers 40 hours of debate in the House of Commons. How many members will have an opportunity of participating in that debate? We will have 288 members in this House after the next election. If one divides 40 by 288 one will get exactly the amount of time available to each member, and one can quickly see that that does not leave very much time for hon. members to speak on this matter.

I will deal with the hon. member for Yorkton-Melville very shortly, but I want to deal now with the government's intention with regard to this bill. To alleviate any doubt there might be in anybody's mind, I would like to quote from certain speeches made by ministers regarding this bill. In a speech made by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lalonde) on the introduction of this bill, he said:
For instance: It could serve to acquaint the large majority of our citizens with the importance and character of proposals for constitutional changes and permit the people to express themselves directly on these proposals. Even if the proposals were supported by the great majority of federal and provincial governments and by the important political parties, such public participation on the process of constitutional change could be very valuable.
Further on in that same speech, he said:
Direct public involvement could also serve to guide the federal and provincial governments, should the process of constitutional revision ever become blocked.
At the conference of first ministers on the constitution last October, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) said:
Once again, what will we do if once again we fail because one of us, or two of us, is not in agreement with the overwhelming majority? Do we just throw up our hands-let some constituent assembly made up of editorialists and professors and legal experts write the thing, we haven't been able to in 51 years, let's give it to somebody else? Or do we consult the people, as a suggestion that has sometimes been made?
The former minister of justice, who is now the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang), stated before the Senate and House of Commons committee on the constitution possible uses of the mechanism for a referendum. He said:
These options indeed contemplate the use of referenda in lieu of consent of parliament as well as in lieu of provincial legislatures. Second, a strong argument can be made for direct voter involvement in constitutional amendment, particularly when government are chronically unable to reach agreement.
Finally, the Prime Minister at a press conference indicated his use of referenda in terms of constitutional change. Theoretically, this government could, on a very broad and important range of issues dealing with constitutional matters of every type and of extreme importance, proceed to use this

device as a very large club in terms of constitutional amendment provisions.
What of the interests of minority groups in this country? I was interested to hear the remarks of the leader of the New Democratic Party who, along with other members of his party, professes to be interested in minority rights. Does his party accept the proposition that the majority point of view shall prevail as implicit in the use of referenda? Is this somehow their idea of protecting the rights of minority groups across this country?
I ask the hon. member for Yorkton-Melville, has he been consulted by his leader about this bill? Has the hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre (Mr. Benjamin) been consulted about this bill? Is there unanimity in their party with respect to this legislation? I challenge the hon. member to stand up and say that he has the full support of his party. I would like to know, for example, where the hon. member stands if the Government of Canada, with regard to our energy needs, decided that it will pursue the question of resource control and taxation in terms of constitutional authority and jurisdiction. What will happen then to the province of Saskatchewan if it has a minority point of view regarding the arrangement in 1930, where by the control of all natural resources was turned over to the provinces of Saskatchewan and Alberta, and this arrangement is rescinded and the resources revert to the control of all Canada? Has Mr. Blakeney discussed this matter with the leader of the New Democratic Party? Is this a matter where they are on all fours, so to speak?
We know the New Democratic Party's position in the coming election. A former member of that party and a man who is on intimate terms with each of its members, Mr. Doug Fisher, wrote an article in which he pointed out that there is absolutely no dout where his party stands in terms of supporting parties in this House; that when it comes to the crunch his party will support the Liberal government and the Prime Minister of this country right down the line. I would like to hear from that party where they stand in terms of this particular bill. Is it just another example of their blind subservience and obedience to the great Liberal party of this country when it comes down to the crunch? I want to hear them in the next election speak about the right to and control of resources. Where will the New Democratic Party stand on that issue?
I know that the New Democratic Party, for example, has very close allegiance with the CLC. I suggest that on occasion the party should be renamed the "New McDermott Party". It is clear that the leader of the New Democratic Party is now relying very heavily on trade union leadership for support in the next election. What is going to happen when the leader of the New Democratic Party goes to Mr. McDermott and says that the government is under considerable pressure to include the right to work as a constitutional right in our country under a charter of rights? There is a substantial body of opinion in Canada that believes the right to work should be included in the constitution. I have met with a number of chambers of

commerce that have made such representations to me, as I am sure they have to many other members. What is Mr. McDermott, the real leader of the New Democratic Party, going to say about that kind of referendum being held in Canada?
What is going to happen if there is a possibility of such a suggestion being endorsed by the majority of Canadians? Of course, then we would have to reconsider. The leader of the New Democratic Party says, "He will fight that. We have 40 whole hours to debate it in the House of Commons. You know what we can do in 40 hours, Mr. Speaker; we have demonstrated we can do it."
There are so many instances of possible abuse under the terms of this bill that I seriously question why any member of the House, including members of the government, should support it. The suggestion or the argument that the bill is limited in scope is preposterous. We are not dealing with a minor question such as whether someone's garbage is picked up in a municipality or whether a school should be built in one area of a province or another; we are dealing with matters of fundamental importance to our country. We are dealing with the constitution, which includes the question of rights, liberties and powers within our government. Let members on the government side remember that the role of parliament is to be a counterbalance against all-powerful governments.
If we in this parliament simply allow this kind of legislation-which arms governments, regardless of political stripe, with powers to involve the country in constitutional changes- to pass, then I say that regardless of on which side we sit we do a disservice to our constituents who have sent us there to represent them.
I want to conclude, Mr. Speaker, by dealing with a couple of other aspects of this bill.

speechtext:
Often in Quebec and elsewhere in this country I find a misconception in that we have grown so regional in our thinking. Some people outside the province of Quebec seem to have grown insensitive to the fact that, as I have said, there are over six million people at the moment who are faced with a referendum. This referendum will be conducted by a provincial government. Surely we are not to deny the federal government the right to conduct similiar referenda on any subject of constitutional importance.
I do not understand the basis for the objections of the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands and the hon. member for Sasfeatoon-Biggar, which I have read, but I will come back to that in a moment.
The fact is that today we often focus attention on Alberta. Alberta is a region. What is important about Alberta? Why we care about Alberta is the fact that there are approximately 1.8 million Canadians in that province, according to the 1976 census. There are approximately 2.8 million Canadians on the island of Montreal and there are as many Canadians that are faced with this menace from the province of Quebec as there are Canadians west of Ontario in the western provinces, including British Columbia.
Let us not lose sight and perspective of what we are dealing with. We are dealing with a very serious and real threat. It is very important to us in the province of Quebec that this law is put in place and put in place soon.
I noticed that the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton (Mr. Baker) in his comments made on December 12 said that we should not move hastily. I do not think haste should be used in the adoption of any law of this importance. I think we should all work together in a non-partisan way to produce a law that

is going to afford the kind of protection to Canadians who live in the province of Quebec which they require.
This bill is consultative. This bill permits the Government of Canada to take the pulse of the Canadian population. This bill cannot bring about fundamental constitutional change. This bill could be referred to, as we often refer to the Quebec referendum bill, as a sophisticated public opinion poll. What more can be read into it than that? Is the opposition saying to us that we are not to know what the Canadian people feel about particular constitutional issues? Would they also like to muzzle private polls, Gallup polls, and Canadian Federation of Independent Businessmen polls which I receive regularly, to find out what business people are thinking in certain areas of the country and communities? That is what this poll is for. Are we to deny the people of Canada the right to express their opinions on matters of this kind?
I would be quite in agreement with the hon. member for Saskatoon-Biggar and with the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands if this situation were to be in any way binding upon parliament. I agree that that would be a denial of the parliamentary democratic system. I am sure everyone would agree with that, and the leader of the New Democratic Party stated it categorically during the course of his comments.
I find this debate quite extraordinary in that I find nothing in this bill other than the right of the federal government, after very substantial debate, in fact more debate than is allowed under the referendum bill of the province of Quebec, to put a question to the Canadian people or to one part of the country for their opinion. It can relate to anything contitutional, but it is certainly not going to change the entrenched provisions of any of our constitutional laws, particularly when it is not binding on this parliament. So there is nothing devious. There is nothing dangerous. I find it extraordinary that the Canadian people should be denied this right.
Accordingly I feel that the debate is somehow getting off track and into areas of partisan politics where it should not be. It is not that kind of legislation. I might also say that the consultative process is very important. However, there may be other ways we can go as well. This kind of referendum bill is certainly one of them.
I felt on this whole question of constitutional debate that we should have involved the muncipalities. I regard municipalities as having an important voice. I know that the Canadian Federation of Municipalities believes it has an important voice and should be speaking on constitutional issues and be at the negotiating table. In a very few years approximately 80 per cent of this country will be urbanized. The powers and the responsibilities of our municipalities are very great. In 1976 municipalities spent 23 per cent of government expenditures in Canada. They should be involved in a very real way. So this is another area of consultation that we should be looking at.
I say the more consultation with our constituencies, the better. That is why I go back to my riding to find out what the people are thinking. Apparently the hon. member for Saskatoon-Biggar prefers not to know what Canada is thinking. I want to know what Canada is thinking on these constitutional
January 26, 1979

issues. I like to know what the mayors and the aldermen are thinking and what problems they have. The more input we have, the better. In the particular issue before us the immediate problem we have is a situation in the province of Quebec which is threatening.
In conclusion, I as a member from Quebec want to underline the significance of this legislation. I ask the opposition parties to share the concern of their fellow Canadians. I cannot emphasize the importance of not permitting this debate to degenerate into bickering and partisan politicking. I ask them to reconsider their views and the impact they can have.
I see nothing in this bill that can in any way be detrimental to the parliamentary democratic process. I prefer that a structure exist that can deal with all constitutional questions and the financing of all referenda so that provision will not have to come up if a referendum is indeed to be debated in this House. It can be debated now and the mechanism put in place so that it will be there for all of us.
At the moment we are dealing with an issue in the province of Quebec. In the future who knows what issue we will want to take the pulse of Canada on in this area of constitutional reform, which is so terribly important to all of us.
With those comments I will terminate my intervention in this debate. I repeat, my point of view may be somewhat different from that of members of the opposition. I put before them the point of view of someone directly involved with the problems of the Quebec referendum. I see nothing in their arguments that lead me to believe that this bill should undergo any alteration whatsoever. I am a listener. I do not believe I am partisan. However, in the arguments I have heard, as we often say in Quebec-

Mr. Speaker, when I called it one o'clock I was being challenged to read on in the quotation I had already started. I see no reason why I should not read on. I was referring to the report of the Task Force on Canadian Unity. The first part of it describes how Ottawa, in the minds of so many, is synonymous with all that is to be deplored about modern government. I continue with the quotation I was reading:
We recognize that this is an unfair stereotype, and that in another 15 years the pendulum may have swung back to the other extreme;
I emphasize the word "may". If this government were in power for another 15 years there would never be a chance- there wouldn't even be a pendulum to swing.
This view of such a widespread appeal today is one of the significant elements which must be borne in mind in any attempt to improve our situation.
We must recognize that. This government does have a deplorable record.
Let us just turn our attention for a few minutes to 1967. Look at our history as it has developed from that time. In 1967, when we were at the peak of our self-confidence and enthusiasm, there was nothing which we in this country could not do. We were, perhaps, a trifle overconfident; I am prepared to admit that. There was not, perhaps, that dash of humility we needed to temper our approach to the future. Maybe that is why we are in trouble today. We lack humility, like certain other people we know in the House who have none of it. Yet genuine enthusiasm existed in those days.
There was enthusiasm to spare about the future, and with good reason. Our material resources were virtually limitless. Perhaps we lacked matching human resources in terms of quantity, but that really meant we would be longer developing that future in the days ahead of us. The only way in 1967 was up, we thought. Now look at us. Only 11 years later unemployment weighs heavily upon us, inflation destroys our earnings and makes us despair of the future. The Auditor General, an officer of this parliament, can see that parliament has lost control of its expenditures, and our national community lies in shreds before our eyes.
We had everything going for us in 1967, and now nothing is going right. We are hopelessly in debt and getting in deeper daily. What have we to pass on to the generations that follow but a monstrous burden of debt? This government has brought us to this pass and it has the nerve to suggest that it should be entrusted with a mandate at this late stage in its career to

reconstruct and reconstitute the institutions of this country in such a broad, general manner, institutions and an economy that have been mauled so grievously.
I think it is time we took a very close look at this particular bill and its terms. The first thing that will strike us is that it does not set up machinery for just any kind of a referendum. It is not designed to find out what I or anybody else in Canada think about the death penalty or about abortion. In fact, such matters are specifically excluded from its ambit, the whole thrust being constitutional reform and constitutional terms. Therefore, it is by way of being a constitutional bill.
It is also aimed, as we shall see, at the Quebec referendum. We heard that pretty clearly from the hon. member for Westmount. But how sharp is the aim, Mr. Speaker? That too we should look at. In essence, the bill proposes a new dimension for political consultation in Canada on matters relating to the constitution of this country. As such it would be introducing, as I suggested, far-reaching institutional changes in our political structure.
Another feature which I hasten to bring to your attention is that the bill bypasses provincial legislatures, provincial governments and provincial electorates on matters which are within the provincial sphere of interest and jurisdiction. In this connection I think it is worth citing an extract from the communique issued on April 14, 1978 by the western premiers conference in Yorkton. It starts out by saying that:
Last week the federal government introduced in the House of Commons the Canada Referendum Act. Section 3 of the bill provides a referendum can be held on "any question relating to the Constitution of Canada or relating to or arising out of a proposed or possible change in the Constitution of Canada."
While the western premiers agreed that it may be desirable for governments to have the machinery to conduct plebiscites on certain matters from time to time, they strongly caution against any attempt by the federal government to substitute this machinery for the settlement of constitutional questions long recognized by constitutional practice and precedents as requiring the approval and consent of every provincial government.
Are we going to override the mandate of one of the constituent parts of this country?

Mr. Speaker, we have to ask why the Prime Minister is intent on going so far in generalities. The main constitutional issue of concern to Canadians at this time is undoubtedly that of the splitting up of our country, which is the aim of the PQ movement in the province of Quebec. Let us recognize that fact clearly and simply. The only referendum question that the government needs to pursue is therefore that of separation. So why introduce such a complicated bill as Bill C-9 and include in it a clause worded as follows, and I quote:
Where it appears to the governor in council that any question relating to the Constitution of Canada or relating to or arising out of a proposed or possible change in the Constitution of Canada is of sufficient importance to warrant obtaining the opinion of electors on that question, the governor in council may, by proclamation, direct that the opinion of electors be obtained on that question by putting the question to the electors of Canada or of one or more provinces specified in the proclamation . ..
Why dodge the issue? Why indeed? The constitutional question which we will need to answer in the next few years is
January 26, 1979

the following: Are we going to live in a federal system, as one country coast to coast, or are we going to let this territorial, federal and political entity be split up? That is the question. That is the question which the hon. member for Westmount (Mr. Johnston) put a moment ago. So let us have a bill which would allow this question to be put to the Canadian people across the country. But let us not come into the House with this multiple choice thing which the government is offering in the form of Bill C-9.

Bearing these particular considerations in mind, we have to examine what sort of constitutional questions are raised or could be raised by a referendum under the terms of this bill. I bet there are many people over there who have never read the bill, and I think it is worth citing clause 2 of the bill, which reads as follows. It defines the Constitution of Canada on which questions could be posed in the following terms:
-(a) the customs, conventions and enactments that comprise the Constitution of Canada,-
It is worded in an elliptical sort of way because it defines it in its own terms. Customs, conventions and enactments are worth remembering. Also:
-(b) the political and judicial institutions and processes of Canada,- are defined in this clause. In other words, a referendum could be taken on any of these matters if any of them or several of them should be "of sufficient importance" in the eyes of the government to warrant consultation.
We are bound to ask ourselves a few questions, such as what is meant by customs. I am not talking about the customs tariff, or anything like that, but rather about customs under the constitution. Is majority rule meant by that? Is it federal-provincial meetings? They are customs, not law. But what about conventions? What conventions might be submitted to a referendum? Would there be a referendum on how to amend the federal constitution? That is still being worked out and there is barely a convention in sight, although there was one once. Would there be a referendum on how to appoint a cabinet? Would there be one on how to select senators and judges? Those are conventions. As to enactments, even enactments can be submitted to a referendum. Would the various acts creating the provinces be submitted to a referendum? What about the Supreme Court Act and the Canadian Bill of Rights?
Then we come to the second portion, political institutions. What political institutions does the government propose to submit to a referendum? Would it be the general election or freedom of the press? What about judicial institutions such as courts of law? What about judicial processes? What does the government have in mind? Does it have in mind trial by jury or the right of an accused to be represented by legal counsel? Is that what the government is trying to do, submit these to
referenda?	...	.
That is what it is trying to do in this bill. The bill has a shotgun approach. While it is true that none of these questions can be put to a referendum before being debated in the form of a resolution in this House, with limited debate of 40 hours,
Referenda
governments with majorities such as the present one have been known before now, and within my recollection of only six years in the House, to force through legislation or a resolution in the face of widespread political opposition in parliament and across the country. Does Your Honour remember capital punishment?
Bill C-9 is being touted as the Liberal government's response to the Quebec referendum proposal. If such should be the case, let the Prime Minister and the government be honest and say so. Why has Bill C-9 been cast in such general terms? Why is it not aimed specifically at the potential threat of separation which Mr. Levesque and the Pequiste movement in the province of Quebec are doing their best to cultivate in that province to the detriment of my country? Why does it not say what it means to say? From my reading of Bill C-9, it seems to have adopted the shotgun approach rather than the single shot approach to a very worrisome question. I do not deny that it is a worrisome question. At this stage in its mandate, I am wondering whether the government has a licence to carry any kind of firearm, whether it be a shotgun or a rifle. Let the government go to the country. Let the issue be specific and go to the country. Therefore, I am wondering whether Bill C-9 is nothing but an exercise possibly in blackmail.
According to the hon. member for Westmount, it is a pure exercise, and the results of it will never be used; we can ignore the results. We are not here to exercise our virtuosity in debating useless bills which will not be used. We are here for a specific purpose, that of setting conditions which will permit the country to develop to its full potential. Yet this sort of nonsense comes before us. It is proposed in the name of one minister when the other minister, in whose name it ought to be, was not in the House to talk to it. He was not in the House when it was introduced, but I am glad to see him present now.
When anything is said concerning federal-provincial relations, who carries the can? It is not the Minister of State for Federal-Provincial Relations (Mr. Reid). Who presided over the discussions in Vancouver? It was not the Minister of State for Federal-Provincial Relations. It was the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lalonde), and he is a sham. The entire matter is a sham.

be given opportunities by the government House leader to take part in the debate. I hope they will have something to say when they participate. Perhaps the Minister of Justice is drawing up the list.
I must ask myself whether this is a purely cosmetic exercise, a gesture aimed at keeping attention focused on one part of Canada's problems, for example, by saying to Mr. Levesque, "If you try anything with your referendum, we will do you one better". I remember singing a great song which has a wonderful tune: "Anything You Can Do, I Can Do Better". This particular bill does not do anything better; it does it a great deal worse.
Are these big stick politics likely to be effective? Have we not had enough confrontation? Has nothing been learned by the government arising from the Kingston meeting held by my leader? At that meeting co-operation and consultation were the spirit of the day, not confrontation. Must we put up with this any longer? Is confrontation the correct approach to constituent governments in a federal system? That is a basic question. Once again attention is focused on one particular question. In any event, it is time to look at something somewhat broader than the Quebec issue. That was all the hon. member for Westmount could talk about, but there are other issues in Canada which are vitally important.
Quebec is not alone in seeking a redefinition of the terms and conditions of its association with its fellow provinces and with Canada as a whole. Unlike the other provinces, Quebec has thrown in another word, "sovereignty". The sovereignty notion was put there by Quebec alone. The rest of Canada rejects sovereignty. Canada is one country. It is my country, and I will see that it stays one country.
Dealing with "association", the second part of that doublebarrelled operation we hear so much about, it is a different matter. Every province in the country wants to have a look at the terms of association with its fellow provinces, the federal government and the federal authority. That is fair enough, and that is what constitutional reform is all about. How many hon. members have looked at the word "constitution"? It is a simple word. It merely means how our country is constituted. It is not very well constituted now, partly because of the confrontational tactics of the Prime Minister and the policies and failures of the government. The constitution of the country deserves re-examination, but it will not be done through a referendum on broad terms like this one. I hope the government is really serious and is not just bringing this bill forward as part of its electoral campaign, which I suspect is the only reason.
This morning we heard about other bills which the government has in mind, such as the Electricity Inspection Act, Bill C-13. Boy, that will be a dinger! At no time did I hear the government House leader say Bill C-9 would be on the floor of this House until it goes to committee. I was wondering, as a matter of fact, whether the government House leader was going to come into the House after lunch and say we will go to the electricity bill this afternoon.
