speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Bill C-9 respecting referendums in Canada is designed to set up the necessary procedures for holding a vote on any controversial constitutional matter. Let us not delude ourselves: this bill is meant strictly to deal with the province of Quebec. For a long time now, at least Social Credit members have been calling for referendums, not necessarily on constitutional matters but on other matters which, to our mind, are every bit as important. We repeatedly called for a referendum, for instance, on capital punishment, but the government refused; it has never been willing to consult the Canadian people as a whole on such an important matter. Still, doubtless pressed by events, probably those of November, 1976, in Quebec, the government has grown alarmed and has decided to have a referendum policy; it has chosen to introduce a bill designed to thwart, if possible, the aims of the separatist government, or that claims to be separatist, in the province of Quebec.
It was especially after the election of November 15, 1976, that we heard a great many public figures make numerous speeches, statements and take a stand on national unity. However, instead of creating more national unity those same people, through most of their speeches and often their actions, managed to provoke even greater national discord because, Mr. Speaker, we are witnessing ever-growing misunderstanding between some Canadian provinces, or at least between one and the rest of the country, between one of the founding nations and the other; it seems that instead of looking for means to placate opposing views, an effort is being made to stoke the fire and stir up even greater dissension. Now, Mr. Speaker, impassioned statements or stay put speeches will never lead to the agreement and the harmony we wish for Canada.
There has been a great deal of talk about national unity. As far as I am concerned, national unity is a myth. When they talk about unity, they mean uniformity, a single option, a common voice. To my mind, we should stress, rather, national
Referenda
harmony. To that end, some representatives of various nationalities and religions could be made to work together towards the self-fulfilment of every Canadian citizen. This might seem like quibbling, Mr. Speaker, but such is not the case, since harmony means much more than unity. For example, a musical group consists of 20, 25 or 30 musicians playing together and producing pleasant and harmonious melodies. But it is clearly impossible to get the same sound out of them. So, in a country like Canada which is no longer made up of only two founding races but of many other ethnic groups which have even improved the very spirit of our country, Canada, I think we must try to live in harmony rather than attempt to achieve a kind of unity designed to cast everyone in the same mould.
Mr. Speaker, according to the drafters of this bill which would allow Canadians to take a personal part in the shaping of a renewed Canada, this is not the only answer, there are many others. But to have the Canadian people speak up, well, we do not know exactly what the government will do once Bill C-9 is passed. There is absolutely no doubt in my mind that it will be, since the government has a majority. Even if all opposition parties opposed it, the bill would eventually be passed, but it is not the only way to allow Canadians to participate in the preparation or the drafting of a new constitution. Some meetings can be held at the government level; in fact, some are held at least once a year. There will be one in a few days. Now, Mr. Speaker, the first ministers who will meet in Ottawa at the beginning of next month are delegated by the population of their province precisely to negotiate, to discuss and reach a consensus on what the Canadian constitution should contain, the constitution that will replace the British North America Act under which Canada was administered since its foundation.
This measure stems mostly from the government's wish to get some working mechanism or means of propaganda, rather, similar to that used by the Quebec government in the present controversy over the country's future. According to rumours and to statements from the present Quebec government, it will benefit from a powerful propaganda machine to sell its position on the future of the province.
The purpose of Bill C-9 is precisely to give the federal government means of propaganda similar to those the province of Quebec has, probably to counterbalance that great debate which will be taking place when? We do not know exactly yet. The date of the referendum in the province of Quebec has not yet been set. We are told that it will be in 1979. If the federal election is called early this year, in early spring, we will probably have that referendum in the fall. We saw, particularly last year, that there was a fight going on between Quebec Premier Levesque and the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) as to who would hold the federal election or the referendum first. It seems that the Prime Minister is losing the battle because his

January 26, 1979
Referenda
margin of manoeuvre is much more limited than that of the premier of the province of Quebec.
So, Mr. Speaker, despite that more or less legitimate objective the government hoped to incorporate four basic principles in drafting the bill. They wanted above all to impose financial controls to ensure a fair and open debate. Furthermore, the bill was to give the referendum process the same level of integrity as the election process. Third, it was intended to respect the federal nature of Canada without giving the federal parties or groups any advantage over their provincial counterparts. Finally, procedures should be as simple and as clear as possible. And in the course of my remarks, Mr. Speaker, I will try to determine to what extent the government has managed to incorporate those objectives in the wording of Bill C-9 respecting public referendums in Canada on questions relating to the Constitution of Canada.
The government limits the scope of referendums only to constitutional matters. It proposes a major legislation paper in which a large number of procedures are discussed in detail. For example, the limits on referendum expenses, the eligibility to vote in the referendum, the air time given opposing groups and federal and provincial parties-in short, the government is about to set up sophisticated structures relating to the referendum. Unfortunately the government restricts the areas where that new legislation will apply. Yet that consultative process of the people could put an end once and for all to several other debates of national importance including, for example, the question of the death penalty that I mentioned earlier.
The result of the referendum would not in any way oblige the government to respect the opinion expressed by the public. That is clearly spelled out in Bill C-9. Mr. Speaker, what would happen if the answer to the referendum of the government of Quebec were to be positive and the one to the federal referendum in that province and on the same issue were to be negative? None of the speeches we have heard so far from members of the government referred to that possibility. What would ,he federal government decide then? Which referendum would prevail over the other, the provincial one or the federal one? Who would decide on that? The Supreme Court? If it is to be so, I think we already know what the answer would be. Mr. Speaker, these are questions we have a right to ask because it is obvious that we are heading toward two referenda. The Quebec government will hold a referendum. The federal government will also hold one on the same subject, and probably in the same province, since I believe that it is up to the province of Quebec to determine its own future within confederation. It is not up to the people of British Columbia or Newfoundland to decide whether Quebec should leave confederation or not. I believe that should be left to the people of Quebec. And if the people of the rest of Canada insist that Quebec remain in the Canadian confederation, I believe that it is not by making speeches, but rather by taking concrete action that they will convince Quebeckers to remain in Canada.

My colleague, the hon. member for Bellechasse (Mr. Lambert), has stated this very clearly yesterday when he commented on the Pepin-Robarts report on the Canadian constitution. He warned the government. He told the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) what should be done to make Quebec or any other province of Canada wish to remain within the Canadian confederation.
Mr. Speaker, I repeat that under Bill C-9, the results of the referendum would in no way force the government to act according to the views of the public. The referendum remains an opinion poll. The government could arbitrarily choose to be bound or not by its results. This means that the government could continue to apply the policy established before the referendum. It also means that if the government had decided before the referendum to take any step necessary to prevent Quebec from leaving confederation and if the people of Quebec voted for separation from the rest of Canada, the federal government could decide to take other action, to use force or to call in the armed forces, for instance. Even if the results of the federal referendum were negative, the government would not feel bound by this decision and could take the action it had decided on before the referendum. And this in spite of the views expressed. We can therefore have serious doubts as to the legitimacy of a purely advisory referendum.
The question asked in the referendum must call for an answer expressed as a "yes" or a "no" as this will simplify the summing up of the votes and reduce confusion among voters. Subclause 3(3)(b) provides for the possibility of asking a question presenting several choices. On that point, Mr. Speaker, I think we should agree that in the event of a referendum the questions must be worded clearly to allow for an answer by "yes" or "no" which indicates clearly to the government the decision which the voters have arrived at in taking part in the referendum. The residents in the province of Quebec are now left wondering. They have yet to know what will be the question in the referendum or how it will be worded. Will it be a brief, clear and plain question or merely a question asking for authorization to negotiate sovereignty association?
Mr. Speaker, an answer at this moment to such a question would be very embarrassing because it would look very much for instance like a vote requested by labour unions before negotiating collective agreements. A union usually asks for a vote of confidence. It asks for the support of its membership. It requests the right to call a strike in order to be in a strong bargaining position before management. Having obtained the right to call a strike, the union then comes up with so many demands that management has to turn them down and it is then that the union will start a strike.
So if the question on the Quebec referendum is put this way, after having obtained an affirmative answer, namely a mandate to negotiate with the rest of the provinces or the rest of Canada, the government of Quebec will then present so many
January 26, 1979

conditions that the rest of Canada or the provinces will have to say no. It will then be very simple, the separation of Quebec will have become a fact. There lies then the danger of having one or several controversial issues in the context of a referendum.
A multiple-choice question offering different alternatives should be put to the people, something the ballot paper must be very clear about. These alternatives ought to allow each elector to vote for or against one of the choices. In all likelihood this would certainly complicate the language of the question. If it were chosen at the time of a referendum, it could undoubtedly extend the debate in the House beyond the 40-hour limit. The referendum question must be approved by the House at the end of a debate not exceeding 40 hours.
Well, Mr. Speaker, I feel that such an important question dealing with the constitution and whether a province should remain within the Canadian confederation requires a very serious debate, and I wonder if a 40-hour debate is adequate to allow all political parties to clearly and fully express their points of view and submit their arguments.
On a number of occasions the opposition parties were accused of filibustering when they tried to extend the duration of certain debates. Well, Mr. Speaker, these efforts may very often have served to provide the public with an opportunity to react and convey to their elected representatives their opinions on the subject under review. When the debate is too short, the public is deprived of this opportunity.
According to Bill C-9, referenda may be held in a province, in a number of provinces, or in Canada as a whole. The government itself will decide the limits of each referendum. I feel that this is dangerous, and we are aware of the risks which people have run in the past with a subject like this.
One should only remember what happened on the occasion of the plebiscite in 1942. We all recall that during that period the province of Quebec in particular was squarely against conscription for military service overseas. People in Quebec were all the more opposed because the government of the day had promised time and time again that as long as it was in power it would not let Canadian sons shed their blood outside the country.
Remember that during the war of 1914-1918 the Conservatives had endorsed conscription and had been booed by the Liberals at that time. In 1939, however, it was the other way around while the Liberals were ruling the province. In 1935, Mackenzie King and his ministers, especially his ministers, all strong men of Quebec, won the election after campaigning against the involvement of Canada in a foreign war. We know how quickly the Liberal government was to declare war on Germany later in 1939. It even did so before Britain. One will remember how the then Liberal government wanted to participate in the war but it had its hands tied up. So Mackenzie
Referenda
King considered holding a referendum in 1942 to release himself from his promises. But the plebiscite was held nationwide, in the nine provinces of Canada. Naturally, eight provinces voted for releasing Mackenzie King from his promises while the province of Quebec voted to hold him to them. So obviously the plebiscite was won by Canada as a whole.
In a referendum on the constitution or on whether Quebec should separate from the rest of the country, if all Canadians are asked to decide such a matter, it is obvious the nine provinces other than Quebec will undoubtedly vote to have Quebec stay. So it seems to me it is useless to spend money to hold a referendum. We already know the answer. The experience of 1942 should make us careful. This particular aspect of the bill will have to be fully debated since it could be used covertly to manipulate public opinion in such a way as to obtain a vote approving the government using the referendum. The legislation should clearly state in what instances every Canadian province and region would be called upon to participate in the discussion and the vote.
The right to vote and the registration procedure would be the same as in a federal election. Several clauses of the referendum bill are closely patterned after the Canada Elections Act while in some respects they are more specific. Mr. Speaker, that part of Bill C-9 is perhaps the most judicious. The expenses for a referendum and the contributions by an individual, a group or a political party must not exceed $5,000. Only registered political parties and referendum committees can make contributions and referendum expenses in excess of $5,000 during the campaign. That part of the bill is unfair to small political parties and minor referendum groups. We should take this into consideration.
Through this exemption, this government accepts to depart temporarily from the principles announced at the outset which are freedom of speech and right of association. It appears clearly that the groups which will have access to unlimited funds for their campaign will be able to publicize their views more efficiently than those with a more limited budget. It is the same situation in a general election. Throughout the political history of Canada we have seen that the political party with the biggest financial support was always the winner. So the situation would be the same in a referendum.
Bill C-9 also deals with broadcasters who shall put broadcasting time at the disposal of registered participants as they do during an election. Half of broadcasting time would be allocated to federal parties on a national scale while the other half would go to provincial parties in every province. This part of the bill might be prejudicial to the democratic process of informing the voters in two ways: first by restricting the broadcasting of a specific opinion, for instance that of the Parti Quebecois, to the province of Quebec and, second, in the case of a debate in which provinces would express partial opinions, the federal government would publicize its views throughout Canada while provincial views would get only

January 26, 1979
Referenda
partial regional coverage. In both cases, the federal government would be highly advantaged in the debate. In that game, Mr. Speaker, the federal government would take the lion's share.
Mr. Speaker, in drafting Bill C-9 it is obvious that the federal government has made sure it will be dealt all the winning cards to obtain the answer it wishes to get. Mr. Speaker, when a question is that important I think that the people of the province of Quebec should be free to give the answer they want to give, to answer freely after due consideration of the consequences of their decision for the future of the province of Quebec and the rest of Canada. It is in that spirit, Mr. Speaker, that Quebeckers should decide because if a decision is imposed on them we will never reach our objective of national harmony.

speakeroldname: Mr. Claude-Andre Lachance (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR HOLDING OF REFERENDUMS ON CONSTITUTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on December 11 last, on the first day devoted to the study of Bill C-9, the leader of the NDP (Mr. Broadbent), in a brilliant speech, referred to the opposition of the Progressive Conservatives to this legislation, saying it was absurd and an abdication of their responsibilities towards Canadians.
Since then, Mr. Speaker, we have heard two other speakers: first, the hon. member for Saskatoon-Biggar (Mr. Hnatyshyn) who, doubtless inspired by the hon. member for Kingston and The Islands (Miss MacDonald), served up more or less the same arguments, haphazardly and pell-mell in a mish-mash that does not even deserve to be dwelt on any longer since I shall soon be discussing the arguments of the hon. member for Kingston and The Islands, official spokesman of the party.
It is however the third speaker on the side of the official opposition I would briefly refer to, because I wonder in particular what meaning some people are giving to the concept of parliament discussing our great national issues. The hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich (Mr. Munro), in an effort no doubt to emulate Jeremiah, heartedly exposed us Liberal sinners. I assume he also includes members from the New Democratic Party because they in their wisdom support the government proposal now before us. The hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich came to the House with his Pandora's box from which he exhibited in succession Saint John's apocalypse, the misfortunes of the Jews in Israel, the most unbelievable horror stories and half quotes. In his highly emotional conclusion somewhat devoid of substance, I thought I noticed a trace of temper, to put it midly, that in my view was not up to the normally elevated spirit of our proceedings here.
Let them address to possible shortcomings in the bill, I'm all for that. Any legislation is always perfectible. This one is no exception, as we have no hesitation in recognizing. Indeed our institutions call for multiple readings. There is the consideration in principle, then second reading at which stage we are

now. But there are also other steps in which a bill can be taken apart and expurged of ambiguities or possible problems, which is perfectly normal and healthy. We have the committee stage for that purpose. It has been suggested for instance that a 40-hour debate is not enough. Well, this can be discussed. Maybe it could be 50 hours, maybe something else. This is no reflection on the principle beneath the bill.
It has been suggested that the ambit of the bill is too wide. Well, this can be discussed in committee to see how it could be narrowed, if we were to take that view. I have no difficulty in envisaging this, and I am perfectly willing that this be discussed. But it is quite another thing to look for intentions, to suggest as did the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich-not only that this will not solve the Canadian problem, on which he is absolutely right and I do not believe the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lalonde) in any way suggested this legislation would solve the Canadian problem, but that the enactment of the bill would bring about the falling apart of Canada. I believe this unjustified projection is going too far.
The hon. member in my view has a long record of service to this country. There is no doubt about that. He served in the Canadian Forces, and he also served in the external service. But then again I did not quite understand the references to sagging morale in our external service. This remains to be proven. As the Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Duclos) stated earlier, our external service is among the best in the world and recognized as such. So much for that. Despite his record, the hon. member feels endangered as an individual by this legislation. I wonder why? This piece of legislation clearly flows from the Canadian government's constitutional authority. Some said the opposite but without providing the least shred of evidence, without undertaking any demonstration of the fact, on the contrary.
Since the Canadian government has the right to introduce such legislation, it can do so one way or an other. The minister and the government decided to draft what is commonly referred to-this expression is unknown in the House or perhaps it has not even been used here in the past-as a general law. That was because the other solution open to us, namely a bill which would deal directly with the issue of the referendum announced by the government of Quebec, was perhaps more difficult to choose at this time. Indeed the form in which this referendum will take place is already known in its broad outlines, because Quebec has also passed such a general law, but its content is still a matter for speculation. I therefore see nothing wrong in the fact that the government wants to provide itself with an instrument with which in due time it will be able to present to the Canadian people or even a part of it, namely a province, a question which will be the subject of a 40-hour debate in the House of Commons, as well as a 40-hour debate in the other place. For those who may not be fully knowledgeable about parliamentary procedure, 40 hours is a lot of time. This represents several days of debate

without the possibility for the government to use closure. Some have said that rather than set the duration of their debate to 40 hours, why not then use the means provided in the present standing orders and thus follow the democratic process as we already know it. It is precisely because if we let the democratic process function as it presently does, these guarantees requested by certain members are not as broad as those contained in this bill because hypothetically one can imagine that in the midst of a debating day at three or four in the afternoon, the government could decide to impose a fixed schedule.
It could well for instance say that we still have two more days to debate the issue and then it will be referred to the Senate for the matter to be expedited. On the contrary, 40 hours in the House of Commons, Mr. Speaker, without the possibility for the government to curtail these proceedings, to limit the right of private members to intervene, this seems to me quite reasonable. Well, we will have an opportunity to talk about it again. Finally, after the opposition have presented its arguments, provided they are more constructive, we may then decide that this delay must be extended. That is quite possible. It will be up to the parliamentary committee to make a decision about it.
Mr. Speaker, this bill does not provide that the question will have force of law once it has been answered by the population in a referendum. Not at all. We are dealing here with a consultative referendum. How does a consultative referendum differ, a mechanism already used in other jurisdictions with the same parliamentary system and the same traditions as ours, whether it be Britain and most of all Australia? I might be told that Britain has used the referendum process in very specific terms through a legislation which was dealing specifically with joining the common market. All right, I agree. But Australia, Mr. Speaker, does have general legislation on referenda which allows her to hold popular votes on constitutional matters. Well, how curious! And it works. It even works rather well and the provinces, the constituent elements of the Australian federation, have never been heard complaining about how those popular votes were working. On the contrary, it is the federal government itself which is complaining, despite the fact that their legislation is more extensive than ours, that the constraints imposed by public opinion and consultation are such that the federal government has its hands tied with those proposed changes to the Australian constitution. What is the idea of trying to make us believe that Bill C-9 will radically change the parliamentary process and corrupt our institutions?
Let us be serious, Mr. Speaker. Once again, if certain provisions of the legislation can cause confusion, we could discuss them in committee. But what is there about the principle of this bill which prevents the Progressive Conservative opposition from supporting it? There is something rather strange in this regard. We talk about consultation. I recall very well that last March, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) sent a
Referenda
six-page letter containing his general proposals for popular consultations to the Progressive Conservative, New Democrat and Social Credit leaders. Did the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) show his disapproval at that time? Indeed not. The Leader of the Opposition is obviously too busy demolishing and criticizing everything indiscriminately to give a specific answer on these political issues. Indeed, since then, he has started to make certain suggestions, with the result that we have seen, especially since his return from a great voyage around the world in 80 blunders, as it was called in the headlines of some newspapers.
Having said this, Mr. Speaker, when the bill was first introduced during the last session, did we hear opposition spokesmen make any great statements about the government's plot to destroy our Canadian institutions? No, Mr. Speaker, not at all! And once again, when the bill was introduced last October, was there any disagreement on the other side of the House? I listened to the speeches and I did not hear any. It is only after the bill was first introduced in the House that the opposition discovered their sacred mission to prevent the Prime Minister of Canada from overthrowing the government. What nonsense! Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich was shocked when the hon. member for Westmount (Mr. Johnston) said: "We have been given a tool in the hope that we shall not use it". He made a terrible scene. However, Mr. Speaker, I repeat that I hope we will not have to use this bill in answer to a referendum in Quebec, and I repeat once more, Mr. Speaker, that those who will not face the facts understand nothing about the situation.
Why should we give it that tool? Mr. Speaker, as I said in the House two years ago, I am one of those who believe that referenda are dangerous if used inconsiderately. I continue to believe that in the first place our parliamentary system was not structured to provide for systematic public consultation, and on the other hand people are not familiar with this kind of consultation, as for example in the Swiss federation. So it is a system which should be used purposely and with great care. I am the first one to recognize it.
Any legally elected government has some constitutive elements of the Canadian federation. A government of an important province in the Canadian federation has dedicated itself to the separation of Quebec and that is in its program, but with that in mind it has promised to hold a referendum to consult Quebec residents. That legislation is now in the books of the National Assembly. The premier of that province has said repeteadly that he will hold one. Perhaps it should already have taken place since they promised in 1976 that it would be held within two years, but as I do not want to be partisan I will say that it will probably take place within a short period. And that is where, Mr. Speaker, as Quebeckers and as Canadians, we will have to face a very serious problem. If only the political philosophy of the Parti Quebecois-a philosophy which like any other political philosophy keeps changing with

January 26, 1979
Referenda
time-were perfectly clear, Quebeckers would not hesitate to answer a clear question.
Then you could say that there is no need for us as Government of Canada to ensure that consultation of the people is carried out properly, for if the question is clear, so would the answer be in the case of a "yes" or a "no". I do not want to enter into the debate of whether after winning the referendum, assuming that it did one day, the government of Quebec can or cannot carry out separation. Some, after examining the books and for purely legal considerations, say "no", they do not have the right while other eminent constitutional experts say "yes", they have the right.
In any case, let us be realistic about the facts, Mr. Speaker. If there was a clearly expressed opinion by the people of Quebec saying "We no longer want to be part of the Confederation of Canada," there would not be much we could do about it. There is absolutely no question about it, and I am among those who believe that the people of Quebec have progressed enough, have enough self-confidence, are aware enough of their responsibilities and duties to make a wise choice, and I will fully respect that choice, Mr. Speaker.
But having said that, the government is a government. I have no intention here, and God forbid that I should, of putting the government of Quebec on trial. But a government is a government, and like any government, the government of Quebec wants to win, and that is perfectly normal. The Progressive Conservatives are a political party and they want to win. The New Democrats and other parties want to win. We are a political party, we want to win. The Parti Quebecois is a political party and a government which wants to win, and that is normal, that is in the logic of things.
Supposing that the Parti Quebecois wants to win and holds a referendum, as the Gallup polls show-a poll is a poll; you cannot make more out of it than what it is-but we are making assumptions and let us hope that the majority of Quebeckers will not be in favour of the so-called separatist option, if there is such an option at this time, because they are not sure-either sovereignty or sovereignty association. There is then an obvious dichotomy between the interests of a government which has to win, they want to win, and a population which is not ready to support an option. This dichotomy leads to the conclusion, namely, that the question, if they must win, if they want to win, must be as nebulous as possible. They cannot ask the question: Are you for Quebec sovereignty? Only one question, like that, because they might very well lose. They cannot ask the question: Are you for the independence of Quebec, with eventually an association? No, they would also lose. These questions are clear, the answer would also be clear.
However, these same polls show that there is in Quebec as in other areas of the country a well-asserted desire to renew the Canadian federation, to give back some authority to the constituent elements, to reform the institutional structures.

Mr. Speaker, this is an easy way out. It will eventually allow them to ask a question if they wish and here again, I do not want to be unfair to the present Quebec government, to phrase their question in such a way that they would get a majority of "yeas". But would those answers be really a victory? Of course, they would see it that way but their opponents would not, they would object that the question was so vague as to make the answer quite worthless, and claim they have no terms of reference to proceed with the separation but only a hypothetical mandate to renegotiate, God knows what. And the Quebec government would say to that: "We have won our referendum!" And they would come here to Ottawa and say: "I want this and that, give it to me I have received a mandate from my people."
What are we doing here as Canadian goverment and as members of parliament? Do we take for granted that the support given to the secessionists is a "carte-blanche" allowing them to go as far as they please?

speechtext:
Oh yes, you can always negotiate and the leader of the Progressive Conservative is good at that. This is no problem for him. He has no authority to do so but he still does.
Our attitude is quite different Mr. Speaker. We fell that the Quebec people ought to decide their own future freely. Once they have decided, we will take our responsibilities. The leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) contends that sovereignty association is just one and same thing. Sovereignty is not bad; it is the association which is important. It is not independance they want, but sovereignty-association, a revamping of the Canadian federal system. Mere presumptions, Mr. Speaker! Nobody knows the actual content of this sovereignty-association. The separatists have never defined it. This may be a new kind of federalism, or a confederalism like some Parti Quebecois experts have said? But two Pequiste members are now talking about a system whereby, although they suggest there would no longer be any Federal or Confederal Chamber, there would be an association freely agreed to, similar to the European Community arrangement or to the Northern Countries Council set-up, which would allow us to continue just like before, whithout any further problems or difficulties. But those are mere the oricians! And again, this is not part of the proposed program of the Parti Quebecois. Even if that were the case, it would mean a radical move from what is now facing us. Is that really what we want, Mr. Speaker? Is that really what Quebeckers want? It will be up to them to decide. But let them decide. Let us not anticipate on that decision even before the question is put. It is unbelievable.
At all events, it is nevertheless natural and sound, and a minimum of caution requires that the Government of Canada provide itself with the appropriate tool to clarify if necessary a situation which could become so blurred that nobody would
January 26, 1979

make it out. But what is wrong with that? What is unusual in that situation? We are told that the scope of the bill is too broad, that it deals with all constitutional matters, but if this bill referred directly to the question of Quebec and the Parti Quebecois, the members of the opposition would say: You single out a particular problem within a province without knowing what is going to happen in that province; you make projections about future events. So, if we did otherwise, they would tell us to do the opposite. And since we do the opposite of what they suggest they accuse us of doing the opposite. Just try and make something out of that!
The NDP has understood what we want to do with this bill. We do not want to destroy our democratic institutions. It was never intended. Anyway, I can assure the House that if any government, this one or any other, took it upon itself to misuse this bill and tried to exert undue influence on the Canadian people in defiance of the House of Commons, there would be such a public outcry that such a government could not function and would be rejected.
Have the Progressive Conservatives so little confidence in the Canadian democracy that they see a threat to our institutions in this legislation which provides the government with a tool to find out what the people think? I have more confidence than that in the people of Canada. I have too much confidence in our parliamentary institutions to suggest that such a piece of legislation will undermine their very foundations. It is unthinkable that one could make such a mountain out of a molehill, and I really mean it. The New Democrats, who do not always share our views and very often criticize and flatten us with all kinds of arguments, but it is all quite fair, have understood the real problem at issue here. But the Progressive Conservatives are so concerned with base electoral considerations that they are blind. Well, Mr. Speaker, we shall proceed with this bill and we will make sure that the question that will be put, either in Quebec or in another context, will be in the best interest of the Canadian people as a whole as well as of Quebeckers.

I wish to say a few words on the bill before us today, Bill C-9 dealing with referenda. I want to begin by saying that the speech made by the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby (Mr. Broadbent), the leader of this party, was "right on" when he gave the position of his party with regard to the bill before the House today. He made it very clear in the debate that we supported the bill before us. He made it clear that we are supporting it because the bill concerns the referendum on the constitutional matter only, and he made it also very clear that we believe the federal parliament needs the power to conduct a
Referenda
referendum in the province of Quebec if indeed the question posed by the Parti Quebecois is not clear. It seems to me that we would be very remiss indeed if we did not give this institution the power to conduct such a referendum if the referendum question in the province of Quebec is not clear.

It seems to me that the Conservative party members are very mixed up and rather inconsistent.
I go back to the speech made in the House by the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands (Miss MacDonald). She spoke about the Parti Quebecois and said:
It is already quite clear that the Pequistes are loading the dice as well as stacking the decks.
If they are loading the dice and stacking the decks, then I do not see why we should want to deny the House the right to have proper legislation allowing it to conduct a referendum if we think the referendum question in Quebec is not very clear. If the referendum question is clear, that is another matter, but what happens if the Parti Quebecois, when the referendum in Quebec is held in October or November, asks for the power to negotiate sovereignty association and wins? What do we do then as the federal parliament? I ask that question very seriously. I think we should have the power and the right to put a very clear question to the people of Quebec: Are they in favour of becoming independent? The Conservative party may say "nonsense" to that, but I ask them: Who speaks for Canada? I think we all do. We are all a part of this country.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR HOLDING OF REFERENDUMS ON CONSTITUTION
speechtext:
I do not say this with any particular slant against the Parti Quebecois; I recognize they are well meaning, intelligent, capable people. That is one of the reasons why I think they might do very well in the referendum that will probably be conducted next fall. They are brillant politicians, brillant communicators. The hon. member for Kingston and the Islands says they are stacking the decks and loading the dice. They are doing all these things, yet she would have parliament deny us Canadians in general the right to ask Quebec a clearcut question. I do not think that is right. I think we, as Canadians, should have the right to do just that. We are all Canadians.
The hon. member for Westmount (Mr. Johnston) in his speech said this was a real problem where he comes from and that they are concerned about independence. Then a member from Alberta said we are all Canadians, we are concerned about that too. If we are concerned, then why not make sure that this institution has the power to conduct a referendum to clarify things? I think that is fair and straightforward. That type of legislation has been in effect in many countries in the world. In Great Britain, for example, there have been referenda conducted on constitutional matters.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR HOLDING OF REFERENDUMS ON CONSTITUTION
speechtext: Oh, oh!

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR HOLDING OF REFERENDUMS ON CONSTITUTION
speechtext:
If the hon. member does not know what the purpose of this legislation is, then I am really surprised.
We are faced with possibly the greatest crisis in this country, the fact that an important part of the country will be faced with the question about splitting away and becoming independent. The bill before us now will give the federal parliament the power to conduct a referendum in Quebec or in any other province, or indeed if there is a new constitutional package, to conduct it right across this country. That is all this bill is talking about. Some members of the Conservative party think that is funny. I would like to know where they stand.
A few months ago the leader of that party was quoted as saying that if Mr. Levesque gets 60 per cent or over of the vote on sovereignty association, he would sit down and negotiate it with him. I understand he said it in French, but he still said it.
I have seen journalists who have talked to people who were at that particular meeting. I believe it took place in Riviere-du-Loup. That is what the Leader of the Conservative party said. He did not know what Mr. Levesque meant by sovereignty association, but by God he was ready to sit down and negotiate it. He is saying what Levesque is saying: "Negotiate two sovereign countries."

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR HOLDING OF REFERENDUMS ON CONSTITUTION
speechtext: That is not what he said.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR HOLDING OF REFERENDUMS ON CONSTITUTION
speechtext:
Yes, it is. I am glad the hon. member said that, because I was about to indicate that the Leader of the

Opposition then changed his mind. I was not surprised that he changed his mind because he does so often. Now the Leader of the Opposition is saying that he really did not mean that, they will have discussions and talk. What is the difference between negotiating and talking, negotiating and having discussions?
The hon. member for Rosedale (Mr. Crombie) appeared on CTV's "Question Period". He made it very clear that we should sit down and negotiate sovereignty association, and that it would be very silly not to sit down for such a purpose. It was not until the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker), whom I admire very greatly, was able to get the hon. member for Rosedale in the corner and give him a spanking that he promptly went before the press and said, "Well, I really did not mean that."
Coincidentally I turned on the television and saw the hon. member for Rosedale. He said that he used four words interchangeably: negotiation, discussion, talking, and another word. In my mind they are similar words, yet the hon. member said, "Now I am not going to talk about negotiation. I will talk about talking and discussions". Apparently that is the position of the Conservative party. During the Christmas recess people were approaching me and asking how a federal party could say such a thing, and whether Conservative members were about to sit down and talk about something of which they knew nothing. I indicated that I would not be surprised, given the present Leader of the Opposition. I said, "You can see him now on his world tour." That is the position of the Conservative party, and it does not surprise me.
The bill before the House is a very clear one. It will last for five years. One would think the sky had fallen in if one listened to the remarks of members of the Conservative party. Perhaps they do not know what the bill is all about, perhaps they have not read it. The bill deals only with constitutional questions; they will not ask about the price of rice in China. The bill contains a sunset clause. It will go on for a period of five years and then it dies. Perhaps Conservative members do not realize this.
It is only advisory in nature and a consultative mechanism. As the hon. ember for Westmount said, it is really nothing more than a public opinion poll. Do Canadians not have the right to say what they feel through a referendum on a matter as basic as the constitution of Canada? Do Canadians in the province of Quebec not have the right to say yes or no to a very clearcut question as to whether they want to be independent or remain a part of Canada? Perhaps the people of Saskatchewan should have the right to say yes or no to a certain constitutional package. Perhaps one area of the country should not receive special treatment, as has been suggested by some Conservative members. The bill requests a direct yes or no answer to a very clearcut question. It does not have to apply necessarily to the entire country. It can apply to one province or region of the country. If we are dealing with whether Quebec wants to remain a part of Canada, indeed that is what will happen.
Some members have expressed concern about the fact that 40 hours of debate is not long enough. Surely that is a quibbling question. We must remember that 40 hours repre-
January 26, 1979

sents between eight or ten days of consideration in the House of Commons. I realize it takes Conservative members a long time to say anything, but ten days should be long enough. Once the bill leaves the House of Commons, it goes before the Senate for consideration. Where the 40-hour maximum applies as well. Thus, we are looking at approximately 20 days of consideration. There are only five days in a parliamentary week, so we are talking about four weeks. We will have more than adequate time to consider the wording of the particular question which will be put to Canadians.
An amendment could change this particular clause. Perhaps members of the Conservative party would like to have 45 hours or 50 hours for consideration of the bill, but it seems to me that the 40-hours limitation is not a good enough reason to oppose it. When the referendum is conducted, it will be conducted in the ordinary manner in which an election is conducted in terms of franchise, voting, enumeration procedure, ans so on. The contributions made for the referendum campaigns on either the yes or no side will be limited to approximately $5,000 per contributor. There will be government subsidies for groups on both sides, similar to those provided under the Canada Elections Act. Also some free time will be provided by the broadcasters of the country. Those parts of the bill are very important.
In a question as important as the one which will be facing the country, we as a parliament should have a device to go and ask a very clearcut question if we think the situation must be clarified. The entire question of the unity and the future of Canada is a very, very important one. A debate such as this provides us with an opportunity to express our views as to why the country should be united.
Recently the Pepin-Robarts Task Force on Canadian Unity completed a major study. It made a number of observations and recommendations concerning the country and various items in the constitution which require change. We do not accept all its recommendations, but some of the matters to which it referred are very important and should be accepted by the House.
[ Translation]
Now, Mr. Speaker, I would like to extend my congratulations to the Pepin-Robarts commission. As I said in English, it has prepared a sound report and I agree with many of its recommendations. But, Mr. Speaker, Canada is a wonderful country which was founded both by the French and the British 200 or 300 years ago. Long before the British and the French ever landed here, there were many Indians living in this country, who actually are the very first Canadians.
We have the privilege, Mr. Speaker, of having many ethnic groups in Canada. For instance, in the west there are many Ukrainians, Poles, Germans, Chinese and some Swedes like myself. Moreover, Canada is a very vast country; as a matter of fact, the distance between Vancouver and Halifax is greater than between Halifax and Paris, France, or Halifax and
Referenda
London, England. Canada is also a land of plenty with only 23 million people living in five regions which are very dissimilar: British Columbia, the prairies, Ontario, Quebec and the Atlantic provinces.
But unfortunately, Mr. Speaker, there exists a deep misunderstanding between the five Canadian regions, between eastern and western Canada, between our consumers and our producers, between Quebec and the other provinces, but the deepest misunderstanding is to be found between Quebec and the other provinces. There is a significant cultural difference between them but, Mr. Speaker, the problems that prevail in Quebec and in English Canada are generally the same. We all have the same unemployment problems and the same Prime Minister. Therefore we have many very similar problems. It is for reasons such as those I do not wish this country to break up.

It seems to me sometimes we tend to exaggerate the differences a lot more than we should. Of course there are differences, but there are many similarities as well. Many of the differences in language and culture can be turned into tremendous assets with positive results for all of Canada.
I believe we have the flexibility we need in the constitution as it is now, perhaps with some amendments, and we have talked in this party of the different amendments that should be made to the constitution to make it very clear that the resources come within provincial jurisdiction, giving more power in communications to the provinces, and powers in respect of immigration given to the province of Quebec and perhaps others, and so on. I think that with those types of changes all parts of Canada have enough flexibility.
The province of Quebec, for example, does have the right, as it should, to make sure that French is the official working language of that province. Do they have that right? Our leader has said on several occasions that he supports the general principles of Bill 101. I do not think there is any party in the House which would deny that. Sure, there are some "i's" to be dotted and "t's" to be crossed that some might disagree with, but in general Quebec has that right just as other provinces exercise the right to have English as their basic language of work except, of course, New Brunswick, which is probably the only true bilingual or French-English province in confederation. These things do exist and I think we have flexibility.
I think the big thing that is lacking in this country is not a decentralization of power, which the Leader of the Opposition wants us to have, but a more even distribution of development. For so many years so much of the development has been concentrated in southern Ontario. I suppose if there is a spoiled brat of confederation it is the southern part of the province of Ontario. The freight rate structure has been geared in the main to aid that region.

speechtext: Someone says that is boloney. He must be from southern Ontario. The tariff structure has been devised to help in the main the industrial heartland of this country, which is southern Ontario.

speechtext: How about Oshawa?

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR HOLDING OF REFERENDUMS ON CONSTITUTION
speechtext:
We are talking about southern Ontario and that is, of course, part of southern Ontario. I know the hon. member for Edmonton Centre (Mr. Paproski) might think Oshawa is in the north, but it is really down in the south. Anyway, I know the Leader of the Opposition needs some geography lessons but I always thought the entire caucus had more brains than he and I am very much surprised to find that we have somebody here who does not know where Oshawa is.
Then we have government policies which I think probably have centralized this country to a great extent in places such as southern Ontario. Let me give you a couple of examples of what I mean by that. We have concessions to big companies through taxation, supported by the Conservatives. Most of those concessions go to the large companies, and most of the large companies are situated in the province of Ontario. Most of the public servants are in the province of Ontario, and until recently most of the buildings housing those public servants were in Ontario also.
There are even some government inconsistencies. DREE was established to get rid of some of the inequities and disparities in this country, to help Newfoundland, part of Quebec, the northern part of the prairies and the like. Of course we support the objectives of an organization such as that. Then we have other government plans such as the Export Development Corporation that channels government money into the promotion of our exports. As it happens, of course, most of our manufacturing takes place in areas like southern Ontario, so we have government money coming right back into those areas.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR HOLDING OF REFERENDUMS ON CONSTITUTION
speechtext: Take it easy on southern Ontario.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR HOLDING OF REFERENDUMS ON CONSTITUTION
speechtext:
I am not criticizing southern Ontario. It has been smart enough to have shrewd politicians, shrewd businessmen and shrewd people for all these years, and has obtained that development. What I am saying is that the time has come when we must have more balanced development across this country.
Of course, I think that is happening in western Canada. Through our resources it is exerting its muscle like it has never pxerted it before, and will continue to do so. I think the balance of power in this country is starting to shift. There should be more development in western Canada as it relates and pertains to our resources. I think in Edmonton, Yorkton, and all over, that development must continue and must be accelerated. We must have more development in the Atlantic provinces.
There are a lot of things that could be done in the Atlantic provinces which are not being done. We have relied on the old program of offering a company a large carrot, but once it has gobbled the carrot the incentive to stay and expand is gone. We must develop things that are indigenous to the areas, the fishing industry, and the lumber industry. Other commodities

that are produced there should be processed and manufactured in the Atlantic provinces.
In Quebec all we have to do is look at the unemployment rates to know that large areas of that province have not received their full or fair share of national development money and national development policies.
My friend, the hon. member for Nickel Belt (Mr. Rodriguez), and others, talk about northern Ontario as being the real colony of the south, the colony of Toronto. That seems to be the forgotten region of the entire country in many ways because it is part of Ontario. There is no reason why there should not be more development there with more equal distribution and dispersion of the growth in the province of Ontario. These are the things I think have to be done.
We cannot solve the problems in respect of unity entirely by changing the constitution. I do not think we are going to make the country stronger by a tremendous decentralization of power. The premier of my own province has said that is not the solution. We do not want to set up ten quasi-sovereign states. I suggest that would really balkanize the country completely. I do not see how you create more unity by giving a tremendous amount of power to each of the ten parts. As Mr. Levesque said yesterday on television in New York, talking about the old French proverb, if you whet the appetite you become more and more hungry. I think that is what will happen if you have a real devolution of power toward each of the provinces. I do not think that is necessary.
If we want to create equity in this country and help the outlying regions and the people who have not been helped in the past, we need a strong enough central government to distribute income and opportunity right across the country. You cannot do that by creating a system in this country where you have ten provinces given tremendously more power than they have now. I think that is the way the Leader of the Opposition wants to go. At least that is what he talks about, certainly when he is in the west, and that is what he talks about on many occasions in this House without, of course, clearly spelling out precisely what he means.
I see that I have only two or three minutes left. Let me say there are many people who have suggested that if Quebec wants to go it does not matter anyway because the rest of the country will stay as it is. I think they are dead wrong. As the report of the unity task force has said, we should not use economic arguments to keep Quebec in. Quebec has six million people and lots of resources, and perhaps they could do well on their own. Many people seem to think if Quebec goes it will just fall apart and suffer tremendous economic ills while the rest of the country would merrily carry on. I want to suggest that if Quebec goes that could be the end of the entire country. It could be the end of what is left of the entire country as well.
I am sure it would be tremendously advantageous to the Atlantic provinces to have closer ties with the United States. That would make tremendous sense. I see some members nodding their heads. I can tell you, coming from the west, that there would be a tremendous move among the people of the four western provinces, certainly in the three most western
January 26, 1979

provinces, to become independent. Why should we continue to attach ourselves to the province of Ontario from which we import all kinds of manufactured goods but, in turn, to which we export very little? Why should we continue massively subsidizing the province of Ontario? I suggest that within five or ten years we would see the whole country totally balkan-ized, with perhaps three or four different units, a couple independent and a couple perhaps amalgamated with the United States. May I call it four o'clock?

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: It being four o'clock the House will now proceed to the consideration of private members' business as listed on today's order paper, namely, notices of motions.

speakeroldname: Mr. Stanley Knowles (Winnipeg North Centre) moved:
subsubtopic: SUGGESTED IMPROVEMENT IN PENSION PROVISIONS
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should consider the advisability of amending the Old Age Security Act and the Canada Pension Plan to provide for the pensions payable under these two acts to be available at age 60 to all persons who meet the other requirements of the said acts and who are not in or are prepared to withdraw from the labour market, and also to provide for the basic amount of the pension payable under the Old Age Security Act, at age 60 for those not in the labour market and to everyone at age 65, to be increased to $350 per month, for this basic amount to be escalated each year by an amount that will enable pensioners not only to keep up with rising living costs but to share in rising living standards, and also to provide for the elimination of any means or income test from the Old Age Security Act, so that the full pension thereunder will be recognized as the established right of all our people.
He said: I am pleased, Mr. Speaker, once again to have an opportunity to present a motion that calls for substantial improvements in our old age security program. When I ask for improvements, it is by implication to be said that over the years we have done fairly well in building up a program for our older people which is certainly a lot better than was the case a few decades ago. I not only admit that we have done fairly well, I am proud to assert it, for I have been involved in a good deal of the story.
It is a story which gives me great pleasure to tell and I tell it fairly often, but I must not repeat it on this occasion because I would use my 20 minutes and still not finish the story. Even so, I might give one or two highlights to indicate my long interest and attachment to this question. As I have said before, it was actually on the very day that I was born, June 18, 1908, that the House of Commons of Canada first debated a measure having to do with pensions for ordinary Canadians. That was
Old Age Security
the bill which established the Government Annuities Act. I am told that I was born at about four or five o'clock in the morning, but it was not until that afternoon that the House of Commons debated the legislation. So, pensions in Canada and I got started on the same day.
I was also very much aware of the bargaining and the debating that went on in 1926 when the first old age pension bill was passed in this House of Commons and then defeated in that other place, which seems to be on the way out. Everybody is now recommending its abolition. The result of things that year, the bill in the early part of the year and an election and another bill later in the year, was that the first old age pension as such came into effect in Canada in the early part of 1927. That was a pension of $20 per month payable at age 70 under a very, very severe means test. When I first came to this House as a member in 1942, that was still the state of the old age pension, so I have been involved in all the changes that have taken place since, and I am happy to say that many of those changes have been exceedingly worth-while.
We have made things infinitely better for older people today than they were in the days of my parents or my grandparents, days that I remember quite well. Even though we have made these improvements-and I am not taking time to tell the story of the prodding and the pushing that it has taken to get them-the fact of the matter is that there are still further improvements to be made. I am not deterred at all by the argument that this is a time of restraint. I do not feel that that is any reason for leaving until some later year or decade the question of doing something to improve the position of our senior citizens.
Our senior citizens face needs today, even under our improved legislation, and it is my view that this parliament ought to be giving attention to those needs. I realize that this particular parliament, the thirtieth in Canada's history, is in its dying days and that the chances of getting something before there is a dissolution are not great, but I hope that by keeping the flag flying we will get something done on this important question before 1979 is over.
My motion, Mr. Speaker, covers most of the things that need to be done in terms of pension. Perhaps I should address myself to those items in the order in which they are mentioned in the resolution. In the first place it proposes that pensions under the Old Age Security Act and under the Canada Pension Plan should be available at age 60. I emphasize the fact that in neither case do I contend that these pensions should be universal at age 60 the way they are at age 65 but, rather, that they should be available to all those who are out of or are prepared to leave the labour market. In my view that is the only test that should be applied. I do not see the validity of a means test at that age, and even worse than the means test is the marital test that applies to the spouse's allowance which is available to some Canadians now between the ages of 60 and 65.
I know about the campaign to permit people to work beyond age 65. I am a living example of one who believes in that line of thought. What bothers me is that the campaign to provide

January 26, 1979
Old Age Security
for people to be allowed to work longer years can easily lead to the suggestion that the date for the payment of the pension might be made later than it is. In my view it should be made earlier, as I have said, at age 60. Certainly there are many people who are in the kinds of jobs where they can work many years beyond age 60, 65, or even beyond age 70, but the kind of people I represent in the railway shops, packing plants, textile establishments, steel mills and so on in the city of Winnipeg, are in hard, backbreaking jobs, such that whenever I meet these people, especially at election time, they say to me that staying at work until they are age 65 is very difficult. The thing they plead for most is to get that pension age down, at least on the basis of its being available. So I press this matter.
I remember the long struggle to get the age down from 70 to 65 and the years when we were told that it could not be done, but v/e finally got it, even if it took a year at a time to get it down. I suggest that it could now be put down to age 60 and that that is an objective to which this parliament should commit itself.
There is the fact that with so much unemployment in the brackets of younger people it makes sense to let some of the older people who want to retire do so, to open up jobs for those younger people. I am not asserting that this by itself would solve the unemployment problem, but it does seem to be silly to ask the younger people to live on unemployment insurance or welfare when they want to work, and to require older people to stay in the shops and factories to age 65, when they would much rather have the chance to retire and enjoy the remaining years of their lives. Again, 1 stress the importance of that aspect of the motion, namely, that pensions should be available at age 60.
I have said it before and I say it again: I am not arguing for pensions to be universal at age 60 the way they are at age 65, but in my view anyone who is out of the labour market or who is prepared to leave the work force and wants the pension, should be able to get it. That would include housewives at home. So far as women between the ages of 60 and 65 are concerned, especially those who are not spouses-those who are single, widowed or divorced-surely this is the more humane, the more decent way to meet their needs than by that terribly discriminatory spouse's allowance we have at the present time. I press that aspect of the legislation with extreme vigour, Mr. Speaker.
Most of the rest of my motion calls for an increase in the amount of the pension. I have put in a particular figure of $350 per month. That has to be seen in relation to the fact that at the present time the old age security payment, in other words, the basic pension, is $167.21 per month and there is available on top of that a guaranteed income supplement of $137.28 per month, which comes to a possible maximum of $304.49 per month. For persons at that point I am not asking for as much of an increase as I should like to ask. I am simply suggesting a minimum figure. I hope no one in this debate will

argue I have the wrong figure in there, unless he wants to argue that it is too low.
In that connection, Mr. Speaker, you can get almost any figure you want for the poverty level. The committee of the other place that dealt with aging some years ago has, from time to time, through its chairman, Senator David Croll, updated that figure. The Canadian Council on Social Development produces figures on the poverty level too, so it varies. Municipal bodies of social workers produce them also. I would point out that they range all the way from about $5,000 per year to $8,000 per year for a single person, and from $7,000 per year to $12,000 per year for a married couple. I suggest that to anyone who considers the cost of living today, those estimates of the poverty line are not at all high.
It is a fact, of course, that there are some other things available to older people, thanks to the legislation we have been able to win in this parliament and our legislatures, such as health and medical care, senior citizens apartments, and so on. When one looks at poverty levels based on the figures I have given, and when it is realized that the total amount payable under old age security and guaranteed income supplement combined is only $3,648.00 per year for a single person and only $6,756 for a married couple, one realizes that we are still asking most of our older people to live at or below the poverty line. I suggest that is something this parliament ought not to be doing; we ought to be a humane body of men and women and we ought to meet the needs of our older people.
It is argued, of course, that the pension is being indexed according to the rise in the cost of living. Almost every time we raise the issue we get that answer from the government. I want simply to make the statement again that we often make, that the indexing is always several months behind because of the way it is computed. It is also based on a general index and not in relation to the things that senior citizens have to buy. Neither does it conform to the principle I suggest in my motion, namely, that senior citizens should have the right to keep up not only with the cost of living at the point that they retire but should be able to keep up with the rising standard of living which is made possible by the economy they helped to build.
I say it is not good enough to tell us there is this kind of indexing. It does not even keep our older people up with the cost of living, let alone their right to be part of the Canadian family in every sense.
There are those who talk today about lots of older people being wealthy. An organization that I shall not name, because I am shocked at what it said, has suggested this week that perhaps we should abolish universality-we should no longer continue to pay old age pensions and family allowances to everyone. The implication is that there are older people who are wealthy and do not need their old age security. Mr. Speaker, there are statistics which show that 60 per cent of our senior citizens, 65 years of age or over, qualify for part or all of the guaranteed income supplement. You do not qualify for that unless you have little or no other income, Mr. Speaker. That accounts for 1,200,000 of our two million senior citizens.
January 26, 1979

By virtue of the fact that they qualify for the guaranteed income supplement they are already living far below the poverty line.
Above that 60 per cent, that 1,200,000, there are another
800,000	senior citizens. The implication is that they are all right. Mr. Speaker, they are not. I would say that half or more than half of those people are still living at the poverty line or just above it, which is not decent, dignified living.
There may be 10 per cent of our senior citizens at the top, but not more than that, who are receiving enough other income that they do not really need the pension. I suggest the way to deal with them is to raise the income tax on all persons in the upper brackets. Let us not ever go back to the indignity and confusion and bureaucracy of the welfare approach that was involved in means testing pensions as I knew it when I first came to this House of Commons.
I know it is argued that we have more sophisticated ways of doing these things today. It is not as cruel and severe as it was years ago. On the other hand, Mr. Speaker, I say to you out of some experience of knowing what the life of older people was like 50 years ago, and knowing what it is like today, that one of the best things the Parliament of Canada ever did was to put old age pensions on a universal basis; to make them a matter of right and to make them a matter of dignity.
There are older people today, even the ones who may be having a tough time economically, who are better off in terms of dignity and self-respect than was the case for most of our older people 40 or 50 years ago. Let there be no talk of any return to a means test for old age pensions. If there is any worry about the few at the top who make too much and do not need it, it can be taxed back.
The Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) is making some very good speeches about the changes that need to be made in our income tax system in order to get more for those who need it and take more from those who are at the top and do not need it. I go along with that completely. Let us not have the indignity and confusion, the unfairness that existed with the means test as we had it years ago. Once we start talking about the level at which the pension would not be paid, we are in trouble.
I see that I have used my 20 minutes, Mr. Speaker, and that I must sit down. I thank the House for the attention given me as I have made this speech-I do not know if it is the one thousand and fiftieth or the eleven hundredth time I have made it over the years. I am proud of what we have done in the Parliament of Canada to improve things for older people. Let us not stop now just because some people call for restraint. Let us recognize that the older people of this country are part of the Canadian family and that they deserve the best we can do for them.
