speakeroldname: Mr. W. Kenneth Robinson (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
subsubtopic: SUGGESTED IMPROVEMENT IN PENSION PROVISIONS
speechtext:
At the outset, Mr. Speaker, let me say that I am very pleased to follow the hon.
Old Age Security
member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles). As usual, he has made an impassioned plea, this time on behalf of senior citizens. It is the same kind of plea he has been making since he has been in the House of Commons.
I am glad to have the opportunity to discuss this motion today, since it comes at a time when the Government of Canada has just taken some actions to improve the benefits provided to senior Canadians under the Old Age Security Act.
I think, before we directly examine the terms of this motion, it might be appropriate to look at the new changes to see what we are doing, why we are doing it this way, and how much it is going to cost.
In January of 1979 the guaranteed income supplement for old age security pensioners is going to increase by $20 for each household receiving the benefit. More specifically, unattached pensioners, and couples where only one is a pensioner, will receive $20 a month. Where both husband and wife are pensioners, or one is a pensioner and the other is receiving a spouse's allowance, each will have an extra $10 a month.
The other change is a refinement to the spouse's allowance program which will permit the extension of this benefit for six months after the death of the recipient's pensioner spouse.
These changes indicate that the government, indeed that all members of this House share the concerns for older Canadians which are expressed in this motion by the hon. member, although practicality, especially in view of the current economic situation, required a much more modest approach. I think it is particularly significant, in debating the present motion, that we remember this $20 increase will be made not on the basic old age security pension, but on the guaranteed income supplement which is made available to pensioners with relatively low incomes. By doing so, we are ensuring that the money that is available for this increase will go to those who need it most. We could have used the same money to make an across-the-board increase in the basic benefit, but the increase would have to have been smaller, and it would have done nothing to resolve the special problem of the pensioner living alone. Using the guaranteed income supplement, we have given as large an increase to this group of pensioners as we have to pensioner couples who have the advantage of being able to share expenses.
One other thing about these new amendments which is important in discussing this motion is cost. The guaranteed income supplement increase will cost about $290 million, and that is a pretty large sum. To find that much money required some hard decisions about reducing expenditures in other valuable programs, so as to avoid higher taxes or increased borrowing.
But that $290 million is absolutely nothing compared to the cost of the hon. member's proposals, which are so large that even it whole departments of government were eradicated we could not find the money. We would have to raise taxes or public borrowing to finance these proposals. I hope to get back to this point later, if time permits.

January 26, 1979
Old Age Security
We have before us a motion which really incorporates a series of proposals which have been made from time to time by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre. I wish to thank him for putting forth all these ideas at once because it gives us the opportunity to discuss the implications of them as a group. As I understand it, the hon. member has asked for five separate items, at least one of which is not entirely within the power of the Parliament of Canada to grant.
First, he wants eligibility for old age security at 60. This would be subject to some test of non-participation in the labour force, and I am not entirely sure how this test would work or whether it would apply only to those between 60 and 65. I am not sure whether the hon. member would want us to cut off from benefits the many persons over 65 who are still in the labour force on at least a part-time basis. Statistics Canada's figures indicate that 182,000 persons over 65 were labour force participants in March of 1978. On the other hand I see no reason to discriminate between the 60 to 65-year-old old age security pensioner and the over 65s on this ground. I do not know whether the hon. member would go as far as some countries, like Belgium and Finland for instance, in enforcing this retirement provision. Those countries apparently deny pensioners the right to work once they start receiving their pension. I do not know if we would ever want to go that far in Canada. There is no doubt that it is less easy for Canadians over 65 to find work than it is for those under that age, but thus far the door has not been shut altogether. Individual employers may set retirement ages but the nation as a whole does not compel Canadians to stop work completely.
Secondly, the hon. member asks that the same thing be done to the Canada Pension Plan, again subject to non-participation in the labour force. This is a task that might be even more difficult to achieve than a reduction in the eligible age for old age security.
It is not just that the Canada Pension Plan is a federal plan subject to provincial consent, so that we would need provincial accord. There is also the difficulty of paying for the benefits. One member suggested in the last session that we could somehow produce the money for all these proposal by slashing other programs, but neglected the fact that the Canada Pension Plan is a contributory program. The cost of the early benefits under the Canada Pension Plan would have to be borne by the contributions of Canadian workers and employers. The current controversy over the funding of the Canada Pension Plan has largely resulted from a lot of misplaced criticisms about the contribution rate. It has always been clear that this must rise from 3.6 per cent to around 8 per cent over the next 50 years if benefits are to continue to be paid, and this does not seem to be an exorbitant price to pay for the type of solid coverage that the Canada Pension Plan provides. However, when you add in the cost of retirement benefits at age 60, then the costs of this plan start rising at an alarming rate. It is true that the major portion of the cost will have to be borne by future generations of contributors, but surely their interests must be of concern to us as well.
Next, the hon. member wants to see the basic old age security benefit raised to $350. I do not want to dwell too much on this suggestion, Mr. Speaker, because I think that all of us want to see senior citizens receive as much as possible and the cost is the only factor with which we have concern. There are some arguments that could be made as to the effects on retirement savings that a jump in old age security benefits might cause, but I am sure that every member of this House would vote for an increase in old age security benefits if only it did not cost anything. But it will cost. The current basic old age security benefit is $164.74 a month, and the budget for this benefit, not counting the supplement or spouse's allowance, is over $4 billion a year.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED IMPROVEMENT IN PENSION PROVISIONS
speechtext: The hon. member is a month behind.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
subsubtopic: SUGGESTED IMPROVEMENT IN PENSION PROVISIONS
speechtext:
Raising this benefit to $350, even without all the extras the honourable member asks in terms of eligible age and removal of income tests and such, would raise the annual budget over the $9 billion mark a year. In other words, it will more than double the price tag of this program, not just for one year but forever. Having raised the benefit, we could not turn around and decrease it again, except perhaps in some circumstances too dire to be imagined now.
Next, the hon. member wants to abolish the income test on the guaranteed income supplement, and by implication incorporate this benefit with the basic old age security payment for all pensioners. Again, cost is an overwhelming factor which has been mentioned, but this whole proposal must be seen in light of the hon. member's basic objection to the income test, which I hope I will have an opportunity to speak on further, because it seems to me to be a very important concept.
Lastly, the hon. member wishes to set up an automatic indexation of these revised benefits by some measure of the Canadian standard of living rather than by the consumer price index as is currently the case. This idea differs markedly from the current system of indexation, which is intended only to maintain the real amount of benefits. If we were to increase benefits automatically by a larger percentage, one that increased the real value of benefits, we would be increasing the real cost of the program over a period of time. This proposal has been made from time to time, and because of the potential cost implications it is one that we would have to weigh carefully indeed.
It is apparent from what I have said earlier on this motion that there are a number of disturbing aspects to this long list of proposals. Certainly the overriding thing has to be the sheer monumental cost of the hon. member's suggestion, and we have had a pretty thorough discussion in the past of what this would mean to the Canadian taxpayer.
But there is more than simply cost involved here. Some of the things implied in this motion by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre amount to a fundamental alteration in the approach that would be taken toward income for the elderly and for other Canadians as well.

January 26, 1979

For example, the hon. member has proposed that we remove the income test which is currently applied to the guaranteed income supplement. What he is proposing really amounts to raising the old age security benefit and abolishing the guaranteed income supplement altogether. In other words, he is suggesting that we abolish the feature of the program that is designed to direct the benefits to those with the lowest income. He appears to be saying that there is something wrong with a program being designed so that funds will be directed to those most in need.
The guaranteed income supplement was introduced about 12 years ago, and I do not wish to take hon. members through all the changes that have been made since then. But I do want to emphasize three points about the original program. The first is that if the same funds as were available for the supplement had been added onto the old age security program without an income test, the benefits provided would have been much smaller. In today's terms, if the $1.25 billion now being expended on the supplement were divided evenly among all OAS pensioners, this would provide each with an extra $50 per month. Each would have about $215 per month. But a pensioner who has only old age security and the guaranteed income supplement to live on would have about $65 less than the $280.29 available now, with the income-tested benefit. In any real situation the cost effectiveness is always going to be important. Universality is also important, however, and a program like OAS which combines a universal benefit with an income-tested supplement may be the best compromise. That is what we have today.
The second point is that the program was and still is not means-tested, if we define a means test as an examination of both income and assets. Instead, the supplement was concerned only with the income of the individual as defined by the Income Tax Act. This avoided the stigma that is commonly associated with programs which examine the assets of the individual. It meant that a pensioner with a low income, but in possession of a few assets such as a house or car, would not be forced to become destitute before being eligible for this benefit.
I know the hon. member is aware of this difference and prefers to call the income test a means test, but we should remember that the major drawback to a means test, as most people understand the term, is the examination of assets. Under the guaranteed income supplement this problem simply does not exist.
The third point about this program's design is that it was originally a temporary measure, designed to supplement the income of pensioners only where they did not have a chance to contribute for ten years to build up a full pension under the Canada Pension Plan, which came into effect in 1966. However, the supplement was so successful and its value was so obvious that rather than being phased out starting in 1976, the program was made permanent. There is a lesson here, Mr. Speaker, and it is that programs like the supplement do have a
Old Age Security
legitimate role to play. Many people are saying that, rather than being abolished, the guaranteed income supplement should serve as an example to be remembered in designing programs for other deserving and needy groups in our society.
There has been mention, for example, of a guaranteed income for other groups, perhaps through the vehicle of a tax credit system. I would remind hon. members that any proposed tax credit would almost have to be income-tested in very much the same way that the guaranteed income supplement is income-tested. The rate of tax-back on a tax credit might be lower or higher than the $1 for every $2 applicable under the supplement, but the principle would be the same, that is, the greater the individual's income from other sources, the smaller the proportion of the tax credit that would be retained by the individual as disposable income. We all know about the new child tax credit in this regard.
Despite whatever governments may do, it should always remain the right and the responsibility of the individual to plan and build toward his or her own retirement needs as he or she perceives them. The idea that the government knows better than the individual and can do better than the individual in the field of retirement planning is not one that we could easily endorse or justify.

Mr. Speaker, like the hon. member who just resumed his seat, I cannot fail to applaud and commend the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) for the pertinacity with which he comes at this problem and the evident concern he has shown throughout the years for the elderly. He takes a very human approach to this problem. He is ever making these urgings.
In times when the Canadian economy is flourishing it is able to meet at least some of the demands that are put forward by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre and by others. He urges, for example, that a pension be available at age 60. It is not quite clear whether these people would take the pension at age 60 if they wanted to go on. I rather suspect that is not so. At 65 it would be there for them as well, even if they remained in the work force. That is one approach, I suppose.
The hon. member complained about the means test, as the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Robinson) has said. In the extension of the guaranteed income supplement and the qualifications to obtain it, there is a process of a means test which I suppose is actually an incomes test. That is fair enough. I do not see anything undignified about that.
If we were able, we in this House would all want to ensure that the elderly of this country live in full comfort for the rest of their years. We would also like to feel that in their working years these people would be able to provide for that on their own, setting aside and not just frittering everything away. That is one of the unforeseen side effects of this cradle to the grave operation in which we have been involved.
I am sure the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre will agree that a tendency has developed on the part of, unfortunately, a great many people to believe they do not have to save,

January 26, 1979
Old Age Security
the state will look after them, they will be all right, and the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre will look after them when the time comes. They believe that when their time comes the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre will urge that their pension be increased. That is not the ethic that belongs to the Canada that his mother, father, grandmother and grandfather knew. It is not the ethic that brought me into the world.
My forebears had to look after themselves out of their own resources and to look after others in the immediate family, such as cousins who had the misfortune to lose one or the other of their parents. That happened in my family. The ethic of that generation is being lost not wholly but partly as a result of the feeling that the government will look after them so they can spend everything they have. They believe there is no need to save. That is unfortunate.
The hon. member's motion is very complex. I will not necessarily deal with all elements in a connected fashion. One element of the motion is that the pension he is suggesting should be indexed by other than the cost of living index. The present cost of living index does not really apply to the elderly. I have urged that there be a special cost of living index for the elderly, one which is more related to their buying patterns and habits. That is something we ought to implement.
There was a change in the cost of living index, the base, the formula, the basket, or whatever you call it, on which the cost of living index was devised. It took place just about two or three months ago, but it did not meet this particular need.
I have learned that in Britain there are two indices applicable to the elderly. One is apparently applicable to couples over the age of 65 and it relates to the pattern of their expenditures. They may or may not own their own home, they may be living in homes for the elderly; they don't buy clothes to the same extent as younger people and not many of them buy ski equipment, yet that element, sports and recreation, is included in the present cost of living index. It is nonsense. There is another index, and I was surprised to learn of it. It is an index which is applicable to single people in Britain who are on pension. Pensions for them are indexed according to a single person's index. I think it is high time we had our statisticians looking into this matter.
When I heard that the index was being worked on I had very high hopes that there would be an index which could very well be applicable to the elderly. It has not been done and I regret this very much. In passing, and since I am talking about the British pension system, I do feel that I would like to emphasize once again here, unrelated as it may perhaps be to the motion before us but still relevant, the plea of those of us who are deeply concerned about the lot of the British pensioners in Canada who are not getting any indexation of any kind in this country.

I know each country blames the other, but surely there is a way of getting down to it. There aren't that many pensioners in that position. I learned that the agreement between the Italians and the Canadians was concluded the other day and I know this will be a great joy to those who lost their sons during the war. I do wish we could get it cleared up so that those British parents who came over to live near their families-their sons or their daughters who had emigrated here-should get the benefit of the increases in the British pension. However, that is a matter which will arise on another occasion.
We tend to overlook the fact that not everybody needs the pension. Many members object to a means test. The suggestion is that if certain people do not need a pension, if they have sufficient assets to make themselves comfortable in their later years, you can tax them like the devil and take those assets away from them. But what you are doing is simply redistributing income. If someone wishes to refuse the pension, if he doesn't need or want it, why should he not be able to assign it either to someone who does need it or make it quite clear that the money is going into the general pot?
As I said before, I hope there is not a single person in this chamber who does not want to ensure that those who are in need in their later years should not be in want. All of us want to make sure that their needs are catered to, to the extent that is possible. Many of us here, either because of our family circumstances prior to coming into the House, or because of the enterprise we were engaged in before we came here, or maybe because of family circumstances since coming into this House, might feel prepared to forgo the pension which might be available to us from the CPP or the OIS. Why should we not be able to make clear that we wish this pension to be available to someone else who is in need?
I am reminded of one comment made by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre which tickled my fancy. He said: "Pensions ought to be available to wives who are not in, or who are prepared to withdraw from, the labour market." There ought to be more wives around here prepared to comment on that remark. Wives are in the labour market whether they like it or not, as far as I can see, from the time they become wives. Husbands who are in the labour market should be able to contribute that portion of a pension for their wives so they can draw a pension in their own right. Why not?

I am talking about those who are able and willing. Let's distribute the income. That's what we are doing anyway. I am prepared to share what I have with those who have less, and I think a lot of people feel the same way.
There are a few other provisions which have not been included in this and which 1 would like to see. For instance, I would like to see tax measures which would waive certain taxes on those who have reached the age of 60 or 65. I think of capital gains taxes, for example. I will not say 60 or 65, even, at the moment, but I have in mind those who are up in years and have retired from the work force. They have saved up a little packet. They may have put it in Canada Savings Bonds, though I hope they put it in something a little more promising that that. They should be allowed to cash those savings without having to pay tax on half of the gains they made. There might even be consideration given to relieving them of other tax or allowing them a special tax rate in their circumstances. These are ways which could be used to ease the lot of those who are in the later portion of their lives.
I have mentioned the business of indexing pensions in Britain. I heard someone say across the way here that there is no law compelling people to stop working. I think there is such a law applying to public servants requiring them to stop work at 65. A friend of mine who was in the militia came to me saying he had reached the age of 60, and a young girl in the orderly office called him in and said: "You are 60, you are finished, hand in your uniform and get out." Why should he? He still has the desire to go on working, contributing to the training of the young folk who want to be in the militia. Why should he have to leave? This is sheer nonsense.
So unfortunately there are some laws which I think should be examined a little more closely. There are people who want to go on working, as the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre does. I wonder why he is not taking his pension. I will tell you why he is not taking his pension-

There is another measure which I think we should consider because I think this motion opens up a great vista of improvements for the elderly who deserve our attention. I see people going around a shopping centre picking up a little piece of meat and seeing it is beyond their means. Even ground meat is becoming too costly. I wonder if there is some means whereby we can refer the subject matter of this motion to a committee where we could break it down into its various components and see if there are not some other ways still open to us, in these times of restraint on the one hand and inflation on the other, to improve the lot of the elderly, those who are no longer in the work force, those who are prepared to leave the work force, and the handicapped.
